sources.title: Major Fleet-versus-Fleet Operations in the Pacific War, 1941–1945

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After rapid Japanese expansion, the Combined Fleet planned an operation against Midway in June 1942.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Yamamoto hoped to draw American carriers into a decisive engagement. U.S. intelligence identified Midway as the principal objective.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Japan sought a favorable fleet battle; Nimitz sought to protect Midway while exploiting advance warning.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The engagement spread across open ocean around the atoll. Scouting aircraft connected widely separated forces.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Nagumo led four Japanese fleet carriers. Fletcher and Spruance commanded three American carriers under Nimitz's operational direction.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: American carrier groups waited northeast of Midway; the Japanese carrier force approached to support the island attack.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The 4 June island strike was followed by unsuccessful American attacks, devastating dive-bomber strikes and Japanese counterattacks.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Fletcher authorized Spruance's early strike while retaining aircraft pending better information. Nagumo faced conflicting demands to rearm aircraft and recover the island strike.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: American dive bombers disabled three Japanese carriers in the morning; Hiryu was mortally damaged later that day.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Japan abandoned the invasion. Four Japanese carriers and the American Yorktown were lost.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The result materially altered the carrier balance, but did not end the Pacific War.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Intelligence created opportunity without removing uncertainty. Scouting, carrier deck operations, navigation and command decisions shaped whether it could be exploited.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: A simple luck-versus-genius explanation obscures interacting causes. The schematic illustrates sequence, not verified ship tracks.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: NHHC provides chronology and intelligence context; the Naval War College study supports analysis of command decisions and incomplete information.

phases.title: Midway attacked
phases.description: Japanese carrier aircraft strike the atoll.

phases.title: Search and launch
phases.description: American aircraft attack; both sides act on incomplete contact reports.

phases.title: Carrier crisis
phases.description: Dive bombers inflict fatal damage on Akagi, Kaga and Soryu.

phases.title: Counterattack and withdrawal
phases.description: Hiryu counterattacks before its loss; Japan withdraws and Yorktown is subsequently lost.

perspectives.name: Chester W. Nimitz and the American carrier command
perspectives.objective: Defend Midway and attack the approaching carrier force.
perspectives.known: Communications intelligence indicated the objective, approximate timing and force.
perspectives.uncertainty: Contact reports did not initially locate every enemy carrier.
perspectives.constraints: Three carriers, aircraft range and the time needed to launch and recover strikes.
perspectives.decision: Nimitz concentrated carriers near Midway; Fletcher and Spruance launched attacks based on scouting reports. These were decisions under uncertainty, not omniscient ambush management.
perspectives.forces: Three carriers, Enterprise, Hornet and the hastily repaired Yorktown, supported by land-based aircraft on Midway.
perspectives.terrain: Open ocean. Weather, distance and aircraft range governed when and where strikes could be launched.
perspectives.logistics: Yorktown's rapid repair after Coral Sea added a third carrier to the American force.
perspectives.outcome: Four Japanese fleet carriers were sunk and Yorktown was lost. Interpretations range from emphasizing intelligence to stressing the contingency of strike timing.

perspectives.name: Chūichi Nagumo
perspectives.objective: Support the Midway operation while retaining capacity to strike enemy ships.
perspectives.known: The first attack reported a need for another island strike; later scouting identified American ships.
perspectives.uncertainty: The enemy's carrier strength and immediate intentions.
perspectives.constraints: Rearming, landing returning aircraft and defending the carriers competed for time.
perspectives.decision: He ordered preparations for another island strike before new contact information changed the situation. Reasons are reconstructed from operational records rather than private thoughts.
perspectives.forces: Four fleet carriers, Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū and Hiryū, with the main battleship force far to the rear.
perspectives.terrain: Operating within range of Midway's aircraft exposed his carriers to repeated attacks from the island as well as the American carriers.
perspectives.logistics: Flight decks could not at once recover the island strike, rearm aircraft and launch against ships; each choice took time.
perspectives.outcome: All four carriers were lost. Postwar accounts, including the story that the carriers were five minutes from launching, have been revised by later research.

sources.title: A Soviet mortar team advance at Stalingrad, 1942

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Germany's 1942 southern offensive aimed toward the Caucasus oilfields and the Volga region after the failure to defeat the Soviet Union in 1941.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Army Group South was divided, creating competing demands between the Caucasus and Stalingrad.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The campaign combined resource objectives with control of a major transport corridor. Reducing it to a contest over the city's name is inadequate.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Stalingrad extended along the Volga. The surrounding steppe remained essential to the wider battle.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Paulus commanded the German Sixth Army. Soviet defense included the 62nd Army under Chuikov; Romanian formations held exposed sectors outside the city.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: German forces advanced toward the Volga while Soviet forces defended the approaches and then the urban area.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The campaign moved from the summer advance through urban fighting to Operation Uranus and the destruction of the encircled force.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Soviet learning and organizational reform helped make the counteroffensive possible; no single commander's personality adequately explains it.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The November Soviet offensive broke through the flanks and encircled the Sixth Army.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The remaining German forces surrendered by 2 February 1943.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The defeat damaged German strategic prospects and became a major psychological turning point.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Examine an urban battlefield inside its operational setting. Tactical advances through a city can coexist with growing vulnerability outside it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: German and Soviet postwar narratives both simplified responsibility. Casualty totals depend on whether they cover the city, encirclement or wider campaign.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National WWII Museum emphasizes Soviet adaptation; USHMM places the defeat in the war's broader course. NAM supplies additional operational context.

phases.title: Advance to the Volga
phases.description: German forces push toward Stalingrad amid Soviet resistance.

phases.title: Urban battle
phases.description: Fighting narrows the Soviet foothold but does not end resistance.

phases.title: Operation Uranus
phases.description: Soviet attacks against the flanks encircle the German army.

phases.title: Final surrender
phases.description: The encircled force is defeated in separate pockets.

perspectives.name: Friedrich Paulus and the German Sixth Army command
perspectives.objective: Take Stalingrad and secure the Volga flank of the German southern offensive.
perspectives.known: By autumn most of the city had been taken. The flanks were held by Romanian, Hungarian and Italian armies.
perspectives.uncertainty: The strength of Soviet forces gathering beyond the flanks.
perspectives.constraints: Overstretched supply lines, and orders from Hitler that limited withdrawal and, later, a breakout.
perspectives.forces: The Sixth Army, worn down by months of fighting in the city.
perspectives.terrain: Ruined city blocks favored defenders, while the open steppe beyond the flanks was thinly held.
perspectives.logistics: After the encirclement, air supply could not sustain the army, and its strength declined through December and January.
perspectives.decision: He kept fighting in the city and, once encircled, did not break out against orders. Whether a breakout was feasible remains debated.
perspectives.outcome: Surrender by 2 February 1943. About 91,000 survivors went into captivity.

perspectives.name: Soviet command: Chuikov's 62nd Army and the Stavka planners
perspectives.objective: Hold the city to fix German forces in place while preparing a counteroffensive against the flanks.
perspectives.known: German strength was concentrated in the city, and the flanks were held by weaker allied armies.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the 62nd Army could hold its shrinking strip along the river until the counteroffensive was ready.
perspectives.constraints: Reinforcements had to cross the Volga under fire, and the offensive had to be prepared in secret.
perspectives.forces: The 62nd Army in the city, and fronts to the north and south strengthened by newly formed tank and mechanized corps.
perspectives.terrain: A narrow strip along the Volga inside the city, and open steppe for the encirclement.
perspectives.logistics: River crossings sustained the defense, while the counteroffensive required concentrating forces without detection.
perspectives.decision: The 62nd Army fought a layered, small-unit defense, and Operation Uranus struck the flanks in November. Credit for planning Uranus is disputed in memoirs.
perspectives.outcome: Encirclement and destruction of the Sixth Army, at very great cost to soldiers and civilians.

sources.title: D-Day: The Allied Invasion of Normandy
World War II: D-Day, The Invasion of Normandy

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By spring 1944 Germany had dominated western Europe for four years; Anglo-American offensives in North Africa and the Mediterranean had ruled out an earlier return to northern France. Allied conferences in 1943 shaped the invasion plan, and Eisenhower was appointed to command it in December 1943.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Allies considered a second front in north-west Europe essential to defeating Germany and to relieving pressure on the Soviet Union. Hitler's Directive No. 51 ordered the western defences reinforced, and he hoped that defeating an invasion would free forces for the Eastern Front.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Allies aimed to land, establish a lodgement including Caen, then break out and liberate France. German commanders disagreed over how to defeat them: Rommel wanted to fight on the beaches, while Geyr von Schweppenburg wanted to hold armour back for a mass counterattack.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Normandy was chosen over the shorter crossing to Calais for its beaches, weaker defences and position within fighter range. The Atlantic Wall was nearly continuous only in the Pas de Calais. Inland, enclosed bocage country favoured the defenders.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Eisenhower was Supreme Allied Commander, with Montgomery commanding the ground forces. On the German side, Rundstedt commanded in the west and Rommel led Army Group B. Hitler split the panzer reserve: Rommel controlled three divisions, and four could not move without Hitler's permission.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Americans landed at Utah and Omaha, British troops at Gold and Sword, and Canadians at Juno, with airborne forces on both flanks. Static divisions of uneven quality held most of the coast, but the veteran 352nd Infantry Division, undetected by Allied intelligence, defended Omaha. Only 21st Panzer was within striking distance.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Airborne landings and bombardment preceded the beach assaults on 6 June. Cherbourg fell on 27 June and St-Lô on 19 July, while British and Canadian attacks ground forward around Caen. Operation Cobra broke through from 25 July. The German counterattack at Mortain on 7 August failed, and the Falaise Pocket closed in the third week of August.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Eisenhower launched the invasion in a spell of bad weather that made the decision fraught; he had drafted a press statement for use if it failed. Hitler refused withdrawal and ordered the Mortain counterattack, which exposed his armies to encirclement.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Deception held the German Fifteenth Army in the Pas de Calais. Repeated British and Canadian attacks drew most German armour to Caen, leaving the western sector weaker for the American breakout.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Allies were established in France. The Falaise Pocket was sealed in late August; many Germans escaped without their equipment, but Seventh Army and Fifth Panzer Army had effectively ceased to exist. The campaign ended with the liberation of Paris on 25 August.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign opened the way to the liberation of France and the advance into Germany. The war in Europe continued until Germany's unconditional surrender, signed at Reims on 7 May 1945.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Combined operations depend on deception, air superiority and supply as much as on the assault. D-Day missed many first-day objectives, including Caen, yet put more than 160,000 troops ashore and secured a foothold.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Casualty figures differ between and even within institutional accounts. The date the Falaise Gap closed is given as 19, 21 or 22 August, depending on whether the link-up or the end of resistance is meant. Imperial War Museums credits German defensive skill while doubting any strategy could have changed the outcome.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum covers planning and the landings. Imperial War Museums gives the German command debate and campaign. The Eisenhower Library holds planning and command documents, and Veterans Affairs Canada summarizes the Canadian part of the campaign.

phases.title: Landings
phases.description: Airborne drops, bombardment and assaults on five beaches establish a foothold.

phases.title: Battle for the lodgement
phases.description: Cherbourg falls; British and Canadian attacks around Caen hold German armour in the east.

phases.title: Breakout
phases.description: Operation Cobra breaks through in the west; the German counterattack at Mortain fails.

phases.title: Falaise Pocket
phases.description: Allied armies close the pocket around German forces; Paris is liberated on 25 August.

perspectives.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
perspectives.objective: Land Allied armies in France, build up the lodgement and defeat German forces in the west.
perspectives.known: Air reconnaissance, special forces and the French Resistance had mapped much of the German coastal defence.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the weather would allow the landing, and whether it would succeed; he drafted a statement in case it failed.
perspectives.constraints: A short weather window and a multinational coalition of land, sea and air forces.
perspectives.forces: More than 5,000 ships, airborne divisions and assault divisions from several nations, with Montgomery commanding on land.
perspectives.terrain: Beaches of varying strength, then enclosed bocage country inland.
perspectives.logistics: Southern England was packed with men, vehicles and supplies; by 30 June over 850,000 men had landed.
perspectives.decision: He launched the invasion on 6 June despite the uncertain weather.
perspectives.outcome: The landings succeeded, and by late August the campaign had broken German resistance in Normandy.

perspectives.name: Erwin Rommel
perspectives.objective: Defeat the invasion on the beaches.
perspectives.known: Invasion was imminent, and Allied air superiority would make it hard to move armour once the battle began.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where the main landing would fall; deception convinced the German high command that Normandy was a feint.
perspectives.constraints: He controlled only three panzer divisions, and four more could not move without Hitler's permission.
perspectives.forces: Army Group B, with Seventh Army in Normandy and Brittany and Fifteenth Army north of the Seine.
perspectives.terrain: An Atlantic Wall that was incomplete outside the Pas de Calais, which he strengthened with obstacles and mines.
perspectives.logistics: Air attacks held up fuel, ammunition and reinforcements.
perspectives.decision: He pushed for armour near the coast and strengthened the beach defences; he was away in Germany when the landings began.
perspectives.outcome: German resistance contained the Allies for weeks but could not throw them back. Rommel was badly wounded on 17 July.

sources.title: El Alamein: outfoxing the “Desert Fox”, 1942
sources.publisher: AWM London (Australian Department of Veterans' Affairs)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Italy invaded Egypt from Libya in 1940, and Germany intervened in 1941. In 1942 Rommel defeated the British at Gazala and took Tobruk on 21 June, and Commonwealth forces fell back to a line at El Alamein, which Rommel reached on 30 June. Auchinleck's counterattacks in July stopped him there; Auchinleck was then recalled, and after his chosen successor, Gott, was killed, Montgomery took command of Eighth Army.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The First Battle of El Alamein in July and Rommel's failed attack at Alam Halfa on 30 August stopped the Axis advance. Churchill wanted a victory before the Allied landings in North-West Africa and pressed for an early attack; Montgomery, commanding Eighth Army since August, refused until he was ready.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Montgomery aimed to break the Axis position and destroy its army. Short of fuel and mechanized forces, Rommel aimed to hold a deep defensive position.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Alamein line ran from the Mediterranean to the Qattara Depression, which tanks could not cross, so neither flank could be turned. The Axis protected its positions with deep minefields that Rommel called the "devil's gardens".

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Eighth Army drew troops from across the British Empire, including Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, with Greek, Polish and French contingents, and clearly outnumbered the German and Italian army in men, tanks and guns; Gilbert adds that it held air superiority over the battlefield. Alexander was Commander-in-Chief Middle East. Rommel was in Germany recovering from illness when the offensive began, and command of the Axis army had passed to a subordinate.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Axis infantry and armour held positions in depth behind the minefields. The 9th Australian Division held the northern end of the Allied line near the coast.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Operation Lightfoot opened on the night of 23 October with a heavy barrage, and infantry and engineers attacked to open corridors through the minefields. A week of attritional fighting followed, with Australian attacks in the north. Operation Supercharge began on the night of 1–2 November, and the Axis line broke on 4 November.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Montgomery built up men, training and equipment before attacking. His plan, Gilbert writes, combined a diversionary attack in the south, led by Free French troops, with the main blow in the north, meant to force the Axis to counterattack and wear itself down. When armour stalled in the minefield corridors, he continued an attritional phase he called "crumbling", made a diversionary attack to draw in Axis reserves and paused to regroup before Supercharge. On 2 November Rommel signalled Hitler that the battle was lost; refused permission to retreat at first, he began to withdraw his German units.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Australian drive toward the sea pulled Axis forces north and unbalanced them. Continued attrition used up Rommel's scarce reserves before Supercharge struck, and the progress of the Australian and New Zealand infantry opened the corridors that the British could exploit.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: By late afternoon on 4 November the Axis army was in full retreat. Most of its infantry was captured: the Italian divisions, which lacked motor transport, were left behind. Montgomery's caution let the motorized elements escape, and the British pursued into Libya.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: El Alamein was the British Army's first clear, decisive victory over the Axis. Four days later the Torch landings began, and Axis forces in North Africa surrendered in Tunisia in May 1943.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Deliberate preparation and material superiority can overcome a prepared defence, but only through costly attrition, and a cautious exploitation may let a beaten enemy escape.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The National Army Museum suggests Churchill's "end of the beginning" framing may overstate the battle's strategic weight, while Gilbert calls it truly a turning point, though one whose strategic effect was confirmed by the Torch landings. Montgomery's conduct remains debated. The sources give different force totals and end dates, and disagree on whether Lightfoot opened corridors through the minefields in its first hours.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the British strategic and command narrative and its debates. AWM London gives the Australian 9th Division's role and the RAAF's support. Gilbert's Britannica article adds the first battle, Montgomery's plan and the Axis withdrawal; its loss figures are not used.

phases.title: Lightfoot
phases.description: A heavy barrage; infantry and engineers attack to open corridors through the minefields.

phases.title: Crumbling
phases.description: Attritional fighting wears down Axis armour; Australian attacks draw Axis forces north.

phases.title: Supercharge
phases.description: New Zealand and British troops attack again; the Axis line breaks on 4 November.

phases.title: Pursuit
phases.description: Axis infantry is captured, but motorized units escape west into Libya.

perspectives.name: Bernard Montgomery
perspectives.objective: Break the Alamein position and defeat the Axis army decisively.
perspectives.known: The Axis was short of fuel and mechanized forces and had built deep minefields.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether armour could pass through narrow minefield corridors under anti-tank fire.
perspectives.constraints: Churchill's pressure for an early victory before the Allied landings in North-West Africa.
perspectives.forces: Eighth Army, drawn from across the British Empire with Greek, Polish and French contingents, superior in men, tanks, guns and aircraft.
perspectives.terrain: A front between the sea and the Qattara Depression, with no open flank to turn.
perspectives.logistics: Weeks of build-up in men, tanks, guns and aircraft before the attack.
perspectives.decision: He delayed until ready, persisted with attrition when the armour stalled, and launched Supercharge after regrouping.
perspectives.outcome: The breakthrough came on 4 November, but the Axis motorized units escaped.

perspectives.name: Erwin Rommel
perspectives.objective: Hold the Alamein position against a stronger enemy.
perspectives.known: Eighth Army was building up superior forces opposite him.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where the main British blow would fall.
perspectives.constraints: Shortages of fuel and mechanized forces, and Italian infantry without the motor transport to escape.
perspectives.forces: German and Italian infantry and armour, outnumbered in men, tanks and guns.
perspectives.terrain: Deep minefields he called the "devil's gardens", covering a line that could not be outflanked.
perspectives.logistics: Fuel shortages limited how freely he could move his armour.
perspectives.decision: He was in Germany when the attack began; back in command, he counterattacked, told Hitler on 2 November that the battle was lost and, though refused leave to retreat at first, withdrew his German units.
perspectives.outcome: His army retreated on 4 November; most of the infantry was captured, but motorized units escaped.

sources.title: History Through the Viewfinder: Reflections on the Greatest Tank Battle in History
Kursk, Battle of (Encyclopedia of Modern Europe: Europe Since 1914)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the defeat at Stalingrad in February 1943, Hitler persisted with an offensive in the east despite concerns from commanders such as Guderian. Manstein urged an attack on the Kursk salient, a Soviet bulge between Orel and Belgorod.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Soviet offensives early in 1943 had pushed the German line back to where it had stood in the winter of 1941, and Operation Citadel was meant to regain the initiative. Hitler delayed the operation until July to build up armour and assault guns. It became the last major German offensive on the Eastern Front.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Germans aimed to attack the salient from north and south. The Soviet high command (Stavka) expected the attack and planned to absorb it in deep defences before launching powerful counteroffensives.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The salient extended about 160 miles from north to south and 100 miles from east to west. In the south, the German advance culminated near Prokhorovka.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Both sides concentrated vast forces, with the Soviets holding a clear numerical advantage and a reserve front behind the salient. Model's Ninth Army attacked from the north and Hoth's Fourth Panzer Army from the south, under Manstein's command in the south. Totals differ substantially between the sources.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Soviet forces built up to six belts of fortifications. Good intelligence, possibly including Enigma intercepts passed on by the British, helped them anticipate the attack.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The German attack began on 5 July. It stalled in the north with slight gains and culminated in the south near Prokhorovka on 11–12 July. A Soviet counteroffensive toward Orel began on 12 July and retook the city on 5 August, a second in the south followed from 3 August, and the campaign ended with the capture of Kharkov on 23 August.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Stavka chose to defend first and counterattack later. After the Allied landing in Sicily on 10 July, Hitler told his generals on 12 July that he wanted to move troops to Italy; Menning writes that he diverted the II SS Panzer Corps and ordered Manstein onto the defensive, and LeMO dates Hitler's order to halt the offensive to 13 July.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Defences in depth absorbed the German attack before it broke into open country, leaving the attackers worn down when the Soviet counteroffensives began. LeMO describes a battle of attrition that used up Germany's last reserves.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: For the first time, a German offensive failed to achieve a breakthrough. Soviet counteroffensives took Orel and Kharkov, and the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Soviet side.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Germany could no longer mount a major offensive in the east. For the Red Army, Kursk showed mature coordination of several fronts and effective defence in depth, at an immense human cost to both sides.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Intelligence, prepared depth and well-placed reserves let a defender choose when to shift to the offensive.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Western accounts long relied on German sources, and Menning writes that the full intelligence story "remains to be told". The figures for forces and losses cited by the museum, from David Glantz and Karl-Heinz Frieser, differ widely from Menning's. The label "largest tank battle in history" depends on how the fighting is counted; Britannica applies it to the whole battle. Even the depth of the German advance is given as about 10 and 30 kilometres in the north and south by LeMO, and 10 and 30 miles by Britannica. LeMO argues that the Soviet losses weighed far less on the rest of the war than the German.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Menning's encyclopedia entry gives the operational narrative and historiography. The National WWII Museum article sets out the battle's scale and the Soviet counteroffensive. LeMO, the German Historical Museum's online history, gives a short German account, and Britannica a summary; their force and loss figures are not used. No Soviet-side source was read.

phases.title: German pincers
phases.description: German attacks strike the salient from north and south and meet deep Soviet defences.

phases.title: Prokhorovka
phases.description: The southern attack culminates in a great armoured clash; the Soviets halt it at heavy cost.

phases.title: Counterstroke in the north
phases.description: The Soviet Orel offensive strikes Army Group Centre as Hitler shifts forces to Italy.

phases.title: Belgorod–Kharkov
phases.description: A southern counteroffensive breaks through and takes Kharkov, ending the campaign.

perspectives.name: Erich von Manstein
perspectives.objective: Cut off the Kursk salient by converging attacks and restore German initiative after Stalingrad.
perspectives.known: The salient between Orel and Belgorod offered a target for attacks from north and south.
perspectives.uncertainty: How strong the Soviet defences had become during the months of delay.
perspectives.constraints: Hitler controlled the timing, and after the Sicily landings he withdrew forces and ordered a defensive posture.
perspectives.forces: German armies and armour concentrated for the southern attack; the sources' totals differ.
perspectives.terrain: Defended belts across the southern face of the salient, with the advance culminating near Prokhorovka.
perspectives.logistics: The delay was used to build up armour and assault guns.
perspectives.decision: He pressed the southern attack from 5 July until it was halted near Prokhorovka.
perspectives.outcome: Ordered onto the defensive, his forces then lost Kharkov to the Soviet counteroffensive in August.

perspectives.name: Stavka (Soviet high command)
perspectives.objective: Absorb the expected German attack, then launch decisive counteroffensives.
perspectives.known: Intelligence indicated a German attack on the salient, possibly aided by Enigma intercepts passed by the British.
perspectives.uncertainty: When the attack would begin, since Hitler delayed it until July.
perspectives.constraints: The need to hold the salient long enough to wear down German armour before committing reserves.
perspectives.forces: Several fronts with a numerical advantage and a reserve front behind the salient.
perspectives.terrain: Up to six belts of field fortifications across the salient.
perspectives.logistics: Reserves and fresh forces were assembled for counteroffensives in the north and south.
perspectives.decision: It defended first, then attacked toward Orel from 12 July and toward Kharkov from 3 August.
perspectives.outcome: The German offensive failed, and the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Soviet side.

sources.title: Invasion of Poland, Fall 1939
sources.publisher: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia

sources.title: Polish Victims
sources.publisher: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Hitler's racial worldview called for territorial expansion, living space, in the east. By the summer of 1939 Germany had annexed Austria, the Sudetenland and the rest of Czechoslovakia, and Poland was next. Germany withdrew from its 1934 non-aggression pact with Poland in April 1939, and on 23 August it signed a pact with the Soviet Union whose secret protocol divided Poland between them.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Britain and France had followed a policy of appeasement but were now bound to Poland by a military alliance, and Poland expected them to attack Germany from the west if it was invaded; they did not. On the night of 31 August the SS staged an attack on a German radio station near the border, at Gleiwitz, to make Poland appear the aggressor, and Hitler used it to justify the invasion the next morning.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Germany's plan, Case White, was to destroy Poland and gain living space in the east, with armies advancing from north and south to encircle the Polish forces and converge on Warsaw. The war against Poland was planned as one of destruction from the start: in a speech to his commanders on 22 August Hitler called for merciless warfare, Einsatzgruppen and police battalions were formed to kill Poles who might resist, and lists of prominent Poles were drawn up for execution. The Holocaust Encyclopedia describes the aim of German policy as the destruction of the Polish nation and culture, reducing Poles to a leaderless population of labourers.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Poland's long borders lay open to attack from three sides: from East Prussia and Germany in the north and across the Polish Corridor, and from Silesia and Slovakia in the south. Central Poland is crossed by the Vistula and the Bzura, with Warsaw on the Vistula, and the Soviet Union lay to the east.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Army Group North under Fedor von Bock attacked from East Prussia and the Corridor, and Army Group South under Gerd von Rundstedt from Silesia toward Łódź, Kraków and Warsaw, with Slovak units in a smaller attack from the south and strong air support. The Polish army was only partly mobilised, had few armoured or motorised units and older weapons, and its small air force was largely destroyed in the first days. The National WWII Museum credits Heinz Guderian with the combination of tanks and air support later called Blitzkrieg.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Poland mobilised late, and political considerations forced its army into a disadvantageous deployment: it concentrated its forces in the west to meet the attack at the frontier, counting on its allies to open a second front.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Germany attacked at dawn on 1 September, and in the first days its aircraft bombed towns and villages across Poland; Wieluń was flattened on the first day. German forces broke through the frontier defences and advanced on Warsaw, reaching its outskirts on 8 and 9 September, where the defenders threw back the first tank attacks. Polish units fought hard, as at Mokra, where a cavalry brigade armed with anti-tank rifles fought German tanks. In the largest battle of the campaign the Poles counterattacked from the Bzura into a German flank, but by 19 September they were encircled. On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded from the east, and the Polish government left the country. Warsaw, bombed and shelled, surrendered at the end of the month; Germany and the Soviet Union partitioned Poland along the Bug on 29 September, and the last Polish resistance ended on 6 October after the battle of Kock.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Poland's forward deployment, imposed by political considerations, exposed its armies to encirclement, and its strategy rested on an Allied attack in the west that never came. Germany concentrated armour and aircraft at the decisive points. The Soviet invasion, agreed in the secret protocol, removed any possibility of a prolonged stand in the east.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The encirclement of the Polish counterattack on the Bzura and the Soviet invasion of 17 September, which left Poland fighting on two fronts, decided the campaign. Warsaw's defence held out under bombardment until the end of September but could not change the outcome.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Polish army was defeated within weeks, although it fought tenaciously. Poland never formally surrendered, but the Second Polish Republic ended. Many Polish soldiers escaped to fight on other fronts, and those who stayed built the largest underground army in occupied Europe.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Germany annexed western Poland and placed the rest of its zone, including Warsaw and Kraków, under a General Government headed by Hans Frank. In the weeks after the invasion German SS, police and military units shot thousands of Polish civilians, including nobility, clergy and intelligentsia, and Jews; in the spring of 1940 the AB-Aktion killed teachers, priests and other intellectuals and sent many more to concentration camps, among them Auschwitz. Hundreds of thousands of Poles were deported from the annexed regions to make way for German settlers. Violence against Jews escalated, and Germans murdered millions of Polish Jews during the war. In the Soviet zone mass deportations followed, and Polish officers were murdered at Katyn.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Concentrated mechanised forces and air power could overwhelm an army spread along a long frontier. Geography and the failure of alliances shaped Poland's defeat as much as weapons did. The campaign also shows that from the first days the German war in the east was a war against civilians as well as armies.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The National WWII Museum describes the Polish cavalry's charge against tanks with sabres as a myth: its brigades fought with rifles, machine guns and anti-tank rifles. The term Blitzkrieg is used by both sources, but the National WWII Museum notes that it was applied to the German method later. The sources date the surrender of Warsaw differently, to 27 September (National WWII Museum) or 28 September (Holocaust Encyclopedia).

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Holocaust Encyclopedia of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives the invasion, the Soviet invasion, the partition and the occupation, and, in a separate article, German policy toward the Poles and the killings of 1939 and 1940. The National WWII Museum gives the background, the German plan, the course of the fighting, the Bzura, the siege of Warsaw and the occupation.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Britain and France declared war on Germany in September 1939 after the invasion of Poland, but for months little happened in the west, the so-called phoney war. France, like Britain, expected a defensive war like that of 1914–1918 and placed great faith in the Maginot Line on its border with Germany. In April 1940 Germany occupied Denmark and Norway; on 10 May, as its attack in the west began, Winston Churchill replaced Neville Chamberlain as British prime minister.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Allies believed that Germany would repeat the Schlieffen Plan of 1914 and attack through central Belgium, and they planned to advance into Belgium to meet it. Belgium and the Netherlands were neutral and almost fully mobilised, but there was a gap between their defence lines. The French, whose commander in chief was General Maurice Gamelin, believed the Ardennes impassable to armour and relied on it to secure the right flank of their advance.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: After an earlier plan along Schlieffen lines was rejected, Hitler accepted Erich von Manstein's alternative. Army Group B under Fedor von Bock would invade the Netherlands and Belgium and draw the Allied armies forward; Army Group C under Wilhelm von Leeb would demonstrate against the Maginot Line; and Army Group A under Gerd von Rundstedt would make an armoured thrust through the Ardennes, bypassing the Maginot Line and the best Allied divisions, toward the Meuse and the sea.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The forested Ardennes led to the Meuse at Sedan, where the Maginot Line proper ended, and at Dinant and Monthermé. Beyond the river lay open country and the valley of the Somme down to the Channel at Abbeville. In the north the Channel ports, and finally Dunkirk with its gently shelving beaches and long East Mole, became the Allies' only way out.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Germany concentrated its tanks in panzer divisions; the Allies had a comparable number of tanks, but they were dispersed among infantry units and many lacked radios. The Luftwaffe dominated the skies throughout the campaign. The British Expeditionary Force under General Lord Gort stood on the Belgian border beside the French armies; the Dutch and Belgian armies were large but much of their equipment was obsolete. Among the German commanders, Heinz Guderian led XIX Panzer Corps and Erwin Rommel the 7th Panzer Division.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: When the attack began, British and French troops left their prepared positions and hurried north into Belgium, and the French Ninth Army moved north from near Sedan. The troops holding the Ardennes sector, where the French command expected no attack, were almost without anti-tank and anti-aircraft guns.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 10 May German airborne troops seized bridges, airfields and the fortress of Eben Emael, and the Netherlands surrendered on 14 May after Rotterdam was bombed. On 13 May German armour crossed the Meuse near Sedan and Rommel's division at Dinant; after a two-day battle at Sedan, Guderian broke through on 15 May and reached the Channel at Abbeville on 20 May, cutting the Allied armies in two. Gamelin was replaced by Maxime Weygand. A British counterstroke at Arras on 21 May shook the Germans but could not be exploited. On 24 May Hitler halted the armour short of Dunkirk; the evacuation, Operation Dynamo, ran from 26 May to 4 June, and Belgium surrendered on 28 May. On 5 June the Germans attacked the new French line on the Somme and the Aisne and broke through; they entered Paris, declared an open city, on 14 June. France asked for an armistice on 17 June and signed it at Compiègne on 22 June, and fighting ended on 25 June.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Hitler's choice of Manstein's plan put the German main effort where the Allies did not expect it, and the Allied advance into Belgium played into it. Guderian, characterising his advance as reconnaissance in force, kept moving when his superiors wanted to pause to secure the flanks. Gort began to consider evacuation by sea as early as 19 May. Hitler's halt order of 24 May, which Britannica attributes chiefly to Göring's assurance that the Luftwaffe alone could destroy the trapped armies and to Hitler's hope of a peace with Britain, gave the Allies time to strengthen the Dunkirk perimeter.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The crossings of the Meuse on 13 May and the breakthrough at Sedan on 15 May decided the campaign. The race to the sea that followed cut off the northern Allied armies from the rest of France, and the French command could not close the corridor.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: In just over six weeks Germany overran the Netherlands, Belgium and France and drove the British army from the Continent. The evacuation from Dunkirk saved far more men than Churchill had expected, a third of them French, but the British left behind most of their tanks and heavy guns, and many troops were captured.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: France surrendered and was occupied; Philippe Pétain's government had been formed to bring the war to an end. Britain fought on alone, and the evacuation became a source of national morale. In the occupied Netherlands the German administration murdered hostages and deported most of the Jewish population to extermination camps.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An attack at the seam the defender believes impassable, carried on at a pace the defender cannot match, can break a front and paralyse a command. Concentration matters more than numbers: the Allies had comparable tank strength but spread it out. A defensive plan built on assumptions about the enemy's intentions is only as good as those assumptions.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The halt order of 24 May remains debated; Britannica gives Göring's assurance and Hitler's hope of peace with Britain as reasons and notes that Hitler stopped the armour again after lifting the order. The Imperial War Museums use the term Blitzkrieg for the German method; Britannica stresses Allied doctrine and command, with comparable tank numbers poorly employed, rather than equipment. The sources date the start of the evacuation to 26 May or, in earnest, 27 May.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Basil Liddell Hart's Britannica article gives the plans, the course of the campaign from the Netherlands to the armistice, and the halt order. The Imperial War Museums give the Ardennes attack, Paris and the armistice, and, in a separate article, the Dunkirk evacuation.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the evacuation from Dunkirk and the fall of France, Britain stood alone. Hitler expected the British government to accept a compromise peace, and Germany had made no plans to invade Britain. When Churchill's government fought on, Hitler ordered on 16 July that preparations begin for an invasion, Operation Sea Lion.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The German army was unprepared for a crossing, and the German navy feared the Royal Navy and insisted that the Luftwaffe take responsibility; Hermann Göring was confident that his air force could drive the RAF from the sky. On the British side, Air Chief Marshal Sir Hugh Dowding had argued in May 1940 that sending more fighters to France would lead to Britain's defeat, and his warning had been heeded, though only after heavy losses.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Luftwaffe's aim was to gain air superiority over southern England and destroy RAF Fighter Command, so that an invasion could follow. Fighter Command's aim was to remain an effective force, denying the Germans control of the air.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought largely over southern England and the Channel. German air bases lay in an arc from Norway to the Cherbourg peninsula, and the Messerschmitt Bf 109 escort fighter operated at the limit of its range over England. The south-east and London, defended by No. 11 Group, were the most hard-pressed.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Fighter Command, under Dowding, was divided into four groups, each divided into sectors: No. 11 Group in the south-east under Air Vice-Marshal Keith Park, No. 12 in the Midlands, No. 10 in the south-west and No. 13 in the north. Its pilots flew Hurricanes and Spitfires and came from Britain, the Commonwealth and occupied Europe, including Polish and Czech squadrons. Göring's Luftwaffe attacked with three air fleets. Thousands of volunteers of the Observer Corps and members of the Women's Auxiliary Air Force worked as observers, radar operators and plotters.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Britain's advantage was its air defence system, known as the Dowding System. Radar, the most advanced in the world, gave early warning; the Observer Corps tracked raids over land; information was filtered at Fighter Command headquarters at Bentley Priory and passed to group headquarters and sector stations, which scrambled and directed the fighters by radio. Dowding had built it on the London air defence system of 1917 and had backed the development of radar and of the Hurricane and Spitfire in the 1930s.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: From 10 July the Luftwaffe attacked convoys and ports. On 13 August it opened its main offensive, Eagle Attack, against airfields, radar stations and aircraft factories. In the critical phase, from the last week of August to the first week of September, the airfields of the south-east were badly damaged, and 31 August was Fighter Command's worst day. After British bombers raided Berlin, Hitler ordered the Luftwaffe to switch its attacks to London, which was bombed from 7 September. On 15 September Fighter Command repelled another massive attack. Hitler ordered the invasion shipping dispersed on 19 September and on 12 October postponed the operation for the winter, while the Luftwaffe turned to night raids on British cities.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Dowding's defence of his fighter strength in May and his management of limited resources through the control system allowed Fighter Command to fight on; Britannica notes that Hurricanes were used against the bombers and Spitfires against the escorts. Hitler's decision to switch the attack to London, in anger at the raid on Berlin, relieved the pressure on No. 11 Group's airfields. The Luftwaffe had no consistent plan and changed targets repeatedly.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The switch to London on 7 September gave the British defences time to recover, and the repulse of the attacks of 15 September showed that the Luftwaffe could not gain air superiority. By mid-September British fighters were destroying German bombers faster than German industry could replace them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Luftwaffe failed to secure control of the skies over southern England, and Hitler postponed the invasion indefinitely. The Imperial War Museums call the outcome a decisive but defensive victory: Britain stayed in the war.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The night raids of the Blitz on London, Coventry, Liverpool and other cities went on for months, causing many civilian deaths and great hardship, but did little to further an invasion. Germany turned to a blockade by submarine and to the invasion of the Soviet Union. Britain remained the base from which the Allies would launch the invasion of Europe in 1944. Dowding was relieved of his command in November 1940, criticised for not using the larger fighter formations known as the Big Wing, for the weakness of night defence and for failing to resolve the quarrel between Park and Leigh-Mallory.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An integrated system of detection, communication and control can multiply a smaller force by putting it in the right place at the right time. Preserving that force, rather than spending it in a lost battle, can be decisive. The attacker's overestimation of the damage it was causing, and its changes of target, show the cost of poor intelligence and an inconsistent plan.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: How close Fighter Command came to defeat is debated. Britannica writes that by late August it was losing fighters and experienced pilots at an unsustainable rate and that No. 11 Group was fighting for its life; the Imperial War Museums stress that the Luftwaffe overestimated the damage it caused and that Fighter Command was bruised but not broken. The RAF Museum describes the Big Wing dispute that contributed to Dowding's removal. The sources end the battle in September (Britannica) or October (Imperial War Museums).

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Imperial War Museums give the German plan, the Dowding System, the phases of the battle and its significance. Britannica gives the German decisions, the forces, the course of the battle and the Blitz. The RAF Museum's account of Dowding gives his preparation of the air defences, his letter of May 1940 and his removal.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Since the 1920s the destruction of the Soviet Union and the seizure of its land as living space for German settlement had been core Nazi aims. Hitler treated the 1939 pact with the Soviet Union as a temporary expedient. In July 1940, weeks after the fall of France, he decided to attack the following year, and on 18 December 1940 he signed Directive 21 for Operation Barbarossa.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The German military and police planned a war of annihilation against the Soviet state and its citizens, especially Jews. Einsatzgruppen, mobile killing units, were arranged to operate behind the front, occupation policy foresaw the starvation of vast numbers of Soviet civilians, and the conquest and enslavement of the Slavic population was to follow victory. The Imperial War Museums record the Commissar Order, which sanctioned the execution of captured political officers. The invasion, planned for May, was delayed to late June by the campaigns in Yugoslavia and Greece.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The German plan was to destroy the Red Army in the west of the country and advance to a line from Archangel to Astrakhan within about ten weeks. Army Group North was to take the Baltic states and Leningrad, Army Group Centre Minsk, Smolensk and Moscow, and Army Group South Ukraine, Kiev and the Donets Basin. Hitler and the army command expected the Soviet state to collapse within months.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The front stretched from the Baltic to the Black Sea, divided by the Pripet Marshes. Beyond lay vast distances, forests, marshes and rivers, and dirt roads that turned to mud after rain. Soviet railways used a different gauge, so German rolling stock could not run on them. The autumn mud, the rasputitsa, and an early and severe winter later stopped the advance.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Three army groups attacked: Wilhelm von Leeb's in the north, Fedor von Bock's in the centre with the panzer groups of Heinz Guderian and Hermann Hoth, and Gerd von Rundstedt's in the south with Ewald von Kleist's panzer group, joined by Finnish and Romanian troops and later by Italian, Hungarian, Slovak and Croatian units. It was the largest invasion force to date. The Red Army had large forces on the frontier, many obsolete aircraft and tanks but also the new T-34 and KV-1. German intelligence badly underestimated the reserves that the Soviet Union could raise.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Stalin did not believe that Hitler would attack so soon and ignored warnings of the German build-up; Soviet troops were under orders not to provoke the Germans. The invasion achieved almost complete tactical surprise, and much of the Soviet air force was destroyed on the ground on the first day.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The invasion began on 22 June. By 28 June the panzer groups had encircled Soviet armies around Białystok and Minsk, and in July they closed another pocket at Smolensk, although Soviet troops escaped from both. Resistance stiffened, and a Soviet counterattack retook the German salient at Yelnya. On 21 August Hitler gave priority to Ukraine, sending Guderian's armour south; by the end of September Kiev had fallen and five Soviet armies had been destroyed in the pocket. In the north Leningrad was cut off and besieged. Operation Typhoon against Moscow opened on 2 October with huge encirclements at Vyazma and Bryansk, but the autumn mud slowed the advance. A final attack in frozen ground brought German units within sight of Moscow in early December, where they were stopped. On 5–6 December the Red Army, under Georgy Zhukov on the Moscow front, launched its first great counteroffensive.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Hitler's diversion of armour from Army Group Centre to Kiev and Leningrad in August won a vast victory in Ukraine but, the Imperial War Museums judge, threw away Germany's only real chance of an outright victory by taking Moscow early. Stalin's refusal to allow retreats led to huge encirclements. In November Bock and the army command chose to press on toward Moscow instead of halting for the winter, believing the Soviets near collapse. The Soviet decision to evacuate industry eastward and destroy what could not be moved sustained the war effort.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Red Army's ability to raise new armies after catastrophic losses, its stiffening resistance from mid-August, the August diversion, the autumn mud and the winter combined to stop the Germans short of Moscow. The Soviet counteroffensive of early December showed that the campaign had failed.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Germany conquered vast territory and inflicted catastrophic losses on the Red Army, but it failed to destroy Soviet fighting power or force a capitulation. Army Group Centre was driven back from Moscow, and the war in the east became a long one that Germany was not prepared for.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The invasion began the Holocaust by shooting. Einsatzgruppen shot Jewish men, Communist officials and Roma behind the advance, and from late July SS and police units, with locally recruited auxiliaries, shot entire Jewish communities; the Holocaust Encyclopedia records that Hitler's decision of October 1941 to deport German Jews to the occupied east began the policy that became the Final Solution. Soviet prisoners of war died in vast numbers in German captivity, mainly through deliberate starvation and exposure; the Holocaust Encyclopedia calls their death toll a deliberate policy of the Nazi state. Leningrad was besieged and starved for nearly two and a half years. Millions of Soviet civilians died under German occupation.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A campaign planned on the assumption of a quick collapse, without the logistics, intelligence or winter equipment for a long war, overreached itself. Underestimating the enemy's capacity to regenerate turned tactical victories into a strategic failure. The campaign also shows that a war waged as a war of annihilation brought mass murder from its first days.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources weigh the causes of failure differently. The Imperial War Museums argue that the August diversion was to an extent militarily sensible but cost Germany its best chance, and they rank Soviet resistance as perhaps the most important reason; Britannica stresses the weeks lost in argument in August, the five-week delay caused by the Balkans and the severe winter. The Holocaust Encyclopedia traces the invasion to long-standing Nazi aims, not to any Soviet threat. The sources date the Soviet counteroffensive to 5 December (Imperial War Museums) or 6 December (Britannica, Holocaust Encyclopedia).

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Holocaust Encyclopedia of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives the aims, the war of annihilation, the mass shootings and, in a separate article, the fate of Soviet prisoners of war. Britannica gives the plan, the forces and the course of the campaign to the Soviet counteroffensive. The Imperial War Museums give the plan, the campaign, the treatment of prisoners and an analysis of why it failed.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Operation Barbarossa had won vast encirclements in the summer of 1941, but the Red Army kept raising new armies and Soviet resistance stiffened from mid-August. In August Hitler diverted armour from the central front to Kiev and Leningrad. With Kiev taken and Leningrad besieged, he turned again to Moscow, believing the Red Army fatally weakened.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Germans had to end the war in the east before the winter; Britannica writes that some German officers thought Moscow unattainable but saw no choice but to press on. Stalin chose to stay in Moscow and appeared at the annual celebrations in Red Square, while much of the Soviet leadership was evacuated to Kuybyshev on the Volga.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Operation Typhoon was to destroy the Soviet armies in front of Army Group Centre and take Moscow before winter. The Soviets aimed to hold the capital behind layered defences while bringing up reserves, and then to strike back.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The approaches to Moscow ran through forests and along dirt roads that the autumn rains, the rasputitsa, turned into mud in which wheeled and horse-drawn transport became stuck. Frost in November hardened the ground but froze weapons, vehicles and men; the winter of 1941 was the most severe in decades, and the Germans had no winter clothing.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Fedor von Bock's Army Group Centre, reinforced with three infantry armies and three panzer groups, attacked with the Luftwaffe already weakened by months of operations. The Red Army's defence was reinforced throughout the battle by fresh divisions, including reservists and Siberian troops from the eastern frontier; Georgy Zhukov commanded on the Moscow front. Soviet air defence fought costly duels with the Luftwaffe over the city.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: A multi-layered ring of defences was built around Moscow, and its citizens were mobilised. The German panzer groups were to open the offensive with new encirclements of the Soviet armies in front of the capital.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Typhoon opened on 2 October, Britannica dating the battle from 30 September. The panzers encircled huge Soviet forces at Vyazma and Bryansk, but the Soviet troops in the pockets fought on and delayed the advance. The autumn mud then stopped the Germans, who paused. In mid-November, with the ground frozen, they launched a final pincer attack; German units came within sight of the Kremlin, and on 2 December a reconnaissance unit got within 8 kilometres of Moscow. The advance halted on 4 December. On 5–6 December the Soviet counteroffensive struck both flanks and the centre of Army Group Centre, and by January the Germans had been driven back as much as 250 kilometres in places; Britannica ends the battle on 7 January 1942.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Bock, supported by the army command and Hitler, chose to press on toward Moscow in November rather than halt for the winter, believing the Soviets to be on the verge of collapse. Stalin's decision to stay in the capital steadied its defence. When the counteroffensive came, Hitler called for every foot of ground to be held, dismissed generals who advised withdrawal, Guderian among them, and replaced the army's commander-in-chief, Walther von Brauchitsch, with himself.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The German advance ran out of strength on the approaches to the city in early December, exhausted, frozen and short of supplies, while Soviet reserves had arrived. The counteroffensive of 5–6 December, launched against an enemy that believed the Soviets had nothing left, turned the German failure into a defeat.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Moscow held, and the Germans lost their chance of a quick victory. The Red Army failed to encircle and destroy the attackers but drove them back from the capital, and the line was stabilised only after weeks east of Smolensk. Both sides suffered very heavy losses.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The defeat ended German hopes of winning the war in the east in one campaign. In 1942 Germany turned to a new offensive toward Stalingrad and the Caucasus. Behind the front the war of annihilation went on: the shootings of Jews by the Einsatzgruppen and the mass deaths of Soviet prisoners of war continued through the battle.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An offensive that continues past its culmination point, with exhausted troops at the end of long supply lines and without winter equipment, invites a counterstroke. A defender who can keep raising reserves and commit them at the right moment can turn a near-defeat into a victory. Intelligence failures, such as the German belief that the Soviets had no reserves left, compound the error.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources weigh weather and Soviet resistance differently. Britannica stresses the mud, the severe winter and the lack of winter clothing, together with the steady arrival of fresh Soviet divisions; the Imperial War Museums rank Soviet resistance and German intelligence failures as the most important causes. The sources date the battle differently, from 30 September or 2 October, and the counteroffensive to 5 or 6 December; their loss figures are given as wide ranges. The brief's points on the Sorge intelligence are not in the sources read.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: John Swift's Britannica article gives the battle's dates, the weather, Stalin's decision and the counteroffensive. Britannica's article on Barbarossa gives Bock's decision and Zhukov's command. The Imperial War Museums give Operation Typhoon, the final attacks, the counteroffensive and its consequences. The Holocaust Encyclopedia gives the German lack of winter preparation and the war of annihilation.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Relations between Japan and the United States worsened through the 1930s over China. Japan took Manchuria in 1931 and began a war to conquer China in 1937; in 1940 it joined the Axis and by 1941 it had occupied all of Indochina. The United States aided China, strengthened its forces in the Pacific and, in July 1941, froze Japanese assets and embargoed oil and other war materials.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Japan, poor in natural resources, saw the embargo on oil as a threat to its survival and resolved to seize the resource-rich territories of Southeast Asia, although this would mean war with the United States. The Japanese records trace the decision step by step: on 6 September 1941 an Imperial Conference resolved, in the name of “self-existence and self-preservation”, to complete preparations for war with the United States, Britain and the Netherlands by the end of October while negotiating, and to go to war if its demands were not met by early October. Negotiations continued through the autumn, but after the Hull Note of 27 November Prime Minister Tōjō Hideki's government gave up hope of a settlement, and on 1 December an Imperial Conference decided on war; Tōjō argued that war was the only way out.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Admiral Yamamoto Isoroku, commander of the Combined Fleet, planned a surprise attack to immobilise the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor at the outset of the war, so that the Japanese conquest of Southeast Asia and the East Indies could proceed unhindered. Its key elements were meticulous preparation, surprise, and carriers and naval aviation used on an unprecedented scale.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Pearl Harbor on Oahu was the base of the Pacific Fleet, with its battleships moored along Battleship Row by Ford Island and Army and Navy airfields around the island. The Japanese task force crossed the North Pacific away from normal shipping lanes to a point north of Oahu.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Vice Admiral Nagumo Chūichi commanded the striking force of six heavy aircraft carriers with supporting ships, and submarines were deployed to attack any ships that escaped. At Pearl Harbor command was shared by Admiral Husband E. Kimmel and Lieutenant General Walter C. Short. The US aircraft carriers were away: Enterprise and Lexington were ferrying aircraft to Wake and Midway, and Saratoga was on the West Coast.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Kimmel and Short had been warned of the possibility of war, with a war warning on 27 November. Short ordered an alert against sabotage and parked his aircraft close together; Kimmel did not extend reconnaissance to the north-west and kept most of the fleet in harbour. Neither expected the base itself to be attacked. Nagumo's fleet left the Kurile Islands in secrecy on 26 November, five days before the Imperial Conference formally decided on war.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At 6 a.m. on 7 December the carriers launched the first wave. Early warnings, a submarine attacked by the destroyer Ward and a radar sighting at Opana, were not acted on. Shortly before 8 a.m. the aircraft struck the airfields, destroying many aircraft on the ground, and the battleships: Arizona exploded, Oklahoma capsized and West Virginia and California sank. A second wave at about 8.50 attacked Nevada as she tried to leave the harbour; she was beached to keep the channel clear. The attack ended before 10 a.m., and the Japanese task force withdrew without being attacked.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Yamamoto's plan staked everything on surprise and carrier aviation. Kimmel's decision to send carriers to Wake and Midway saved them; Short's anti-sabotage precautions left aircraft packed together and easy to destroy. The Japanese left the shore facilities of the naval base and the oil storage undamaged; the Naval History and Heritage Command notes that the shore facilities played an important role in the Allied victory.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Complete surprise in the first minutes decided the attack: most of the damage to the battleships was done in the first half hour. What was not hit proved equally important: the carriers were absent, and the shore installations survived.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Twenty-one ships of the Pacific Fleet were sunk or damaged and a great many aircraft were destroyed, most before they could take off; Japanese losses were light. Americans killed included civilians. All but three of the damaged ships, Arizona, Oklahoma and Utah, were eventually raised or repaired.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The attack united a divided nation and swept away support for neutrality; on 8 December Congress declared war on Japan. Kimmel and Short were relieved, and the disaster led to numerous investigations.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A brilliant tactical surprise can be a strategic error: the attack brought into the war an enemy whose industrial and political strength Japan could not match. What a strike leaves untouched, carriers, fuel and repair yards, can matter more than what it destroys. Warnings are only useful if they are interpreted correctly.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica records a wide divergence of opinion on responsibility: the Roberts Commission blamed Kimmel and Short, the army and navy boards blamed the War and Navy Departments, and the 1946 congressional majority stressed the lack of preparation in Hawaii. It reports that the “back door to war” theory, that Roosevelt invited the attack, found little support among mainstream historians and was further undermined by declassified code-breaking documents, and that there is substantial evidence that he sought to postpone a clash. The Japanese conference records published by JACAR show the decision for war taking shape over three months, with a deadline set in September and the final decision taken after the Hull Note. The brief's question of a third strike is not discussed in the sources read; the Naval History and Heritage Command notes only that the shore facilities were not attacked.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Naval History and Heritage Command's overview gives the background, the plan, the approach, the attack, the losses and the salvage. Britannica gives the diplomatic background, the warnings and responses, the attack and the investigations. Two of JACAR's commentaries on Japanese government documents give the Imperial Conferences of 6 September and 1 December 1941.
