sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the First World War Britain built a naval base at Singapore and emplaced coastal guns against attack from the sea, but no permanent fleet was based there; a fleet was to be sent only when a threat was imminent. Newspapers and politicians called the island an impregnable fortress, the Gibraltar of the East, although its defences had been underfunded for years.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Bogged down in China and cut off from American, British and Dutch oil, Japan resolved to seize the resources of the Dutch East Indies, and it needed Singapore as a base for that advance. The attack on Malaya was part of a wider offensive launched at the same time as Pearl Harbor. Most senior British planners accepted that the island could not be held if the Malayan mainland was lost.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Japanese aimed to advance down the Malay Peninsula and take Singapore from the landward side. The British planned a pre-emptive move into Thailand, Operation Matador, which political considerations prevented from being launched in time, and otherwise relied on the jungle and on defence of the peninsula.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Malay Peninsula is long and covered by jungle, and the main Japanese advance came down its western side. Singapore island is separated from the mainland by the Johor Strait, crossed by the Causeway; the island's coastal guns faced the sea, and the Bukit Timah heights held its supply depots and, with the reservoirs, its water.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Lieutenant General Tomoyuki Yamashita commanded the Japanese Twenty-Fifth Army, well trained and with many more tanks and aircraft. Lieutenant General Arthur Percival commanded British, Australian, Indian and Malay troops who outnumbered the attackers but had little experience, especially of jungle warfare; the IWM notes that British planning was also shaped by racist stereotypes of the Japanese. Force Z, the battleship Prince of Wales and the battlecruiser Repulse, had been sent as a deterrent without the aircraft carrier meant to accompany it.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Percival spread his troops across the whole peninsula, so that the Japanese outnumbered them at the landing places. On Singapore island he expected the attack east of the Causeway, where the naval base lay, and placed his strongest forces there.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 8 December 1941 Japanese troops landed at Singora and Patani in Thailand and at Kota Bharu in Malaya, and bombs fell on Singapore. Japanese aircraft attacked the RAF airfields, and on 10 December sank Prince of Wales and Repulse, which had no air cover. Using bicycles, motor vehicles and light tanks, the Japanese outmanoeuvred the defenders down the length of the peninsula, and the last British troops crossed the Causeway on 31 January 1942. On the night of 8 February, after a heavy bombardment, Japanese divisions crossed the Johor Strait in the north-west against the Australian sector, and the Imperial Guards followed at Kranji. They took Bukit Timah on 11 February. On 14–15 February Japanese troops massacred patients and staff at the Alexandra Military Hospital. With the reservoirs lost and water and food running out, Percival and his commanders decided to surrender, and he signed at the Ford Factory on 15 February.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Percival's dispersal of his forces down the peninsula and his misreading of where the Japanese would land on the island let the attackers concentrate where it mattered. Yamashita chose to attack with three divisions rather than four and drove his troops on at speed; by the end, the IWM notes, he had outrun his supplies and was short of ammunition, and he insisted on unconditional surrender for fear that the British would discover his weakness. Churchill ordered Singapore held to the last man, a political rather than a military imperative.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of Prince of Wales and Repulse on 10 December and of air cover over Malaya decided the campaign's course; on the island, the landing in the north-west on 8 February and the loss of Bukit Timah, with its depots and water, left Percival unable to hold out.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Singapore fell on 15 February 1942 in the largest surrender in British history. Malaya had been lost in under two months.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: From 21 February to 4 March 1942, in Operation Sook Ching, Chinese men aged 18 to 50 were ordered to screening centres across the island on the directive of Yamashita, and those whom the Kempeitai or the Imperial Guards judged anti-Japanese, often arbitrarily, were taken to beaches and remote places such as Changi, Punggol and Bedok and machine-gunned; thousands were killed, and the true number is unknown. The prisoners taken at Singapore were treated brutally; many were held at Changi, and others were sent to build the Burma–Thailand railway. Civilians suffered food shortages and conscription under the occupation. The loss began the long decline of British prestige in Asia, and Australia turned increasingly to the United States.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Speed and initiative can defeat a larger but inexperienced and dispersed defender. Capital ships without air cover are vulnerable to aircraft. A fortress that exists mainly in propaganda, without the fleet, aircraft and landward defences it depends on, cannot be held once its approaches are lost.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The IWM argues that Percival made mistakes but was badly let down by superiors who had underfunded the defences for years. The sources qualify the popular idea that Singapore's guns pointed the wrong way: the IWM notes that the coastal artillery was designed against attack from the sea and had few high-explosive shells, while the National Library Board notes that the British army had anticipated a landward attack and planned Operation Matador to meet it. The sources give different strengths for the two armies. The National Library Board notes that the death toll of the Sook Ching is unknown, with estimates differing widely.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Imperial War Museums' account by Stephen Walton gives the strategic background, the forces, the campaign, the surrender and its consequences. The National Library Board of Singapore's Infopedia gives the battle for the island, the Alexandra Hospital massacre and the surrender, and, in a separate article, Operation Sook Ching and its aftermath.

sources.title: Battle of the Coral Sea, 4-8 May 1942: Summary

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Pearl Harbor Japanese forces expanded rapidly across the Pacific and South-east Asia. By April 1942 Japan had established a defensive perimeter and sought to extend it.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Japan planned to advance south-east from the Bismarcks and Solomons and seize control of the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, establishing air bases at Port Moresby in New Guinea and Tulagi in the Solomons. Allied signals intelligence uncovered the plan to take Port Moresby, and all available Allied sea and air power was alerted.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Japanese aimed to take Tulagi and then land at Port Moresby, with a carrier strike force to find and destroy the Allied naval forces that came to oppose them. The Allies aimed to stop the invasion of Port Moresby.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought over the Coral Sea, between New Guinea, the Solomons and Australia. The opposing carrier forces searched for each other over wide areas of ocean, and their ships never came within sight of each other.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Two US carrier task forces, built around Yorktown and Lexington under Rear Admiral Frank J. Fletcher, and a combined US–Australian cruiser force that included HMAS Australia and Hobart, faced the Japanese Carrier Strike Force with the fleet carriers Shōkaku and Zuikaku, supporting units and the invasion force from Rabaul, and the light carrier Shōhō.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: When the Japanese landed at Tulagi on 3 May, aircraft from Fletcher's task force struck the landing group on 4 May. The invasion force left Rabaul for Port Moresby, and its covering units took a route that invited a clash with Fletcher. The Allied cruisers were detached to guard against the Port Moresby invasion force.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 5 and 6 May the carrier groups searched for each other. On the morning of 7 May Japanese aircraft sank the destroyer Sims and the oiler Neosho, while Fletcher's aircraft sank the light carrier Shōhō and a cruiser. On 8 May both sides struck at each other's carriers: Japanese aircraft sank Lexington, which was abandoned after explosions and fires, and damaged Yorktown, while US aircraft damaged Shōkaku so badly that she had to retire. With its air cover weakened and under attack by Allied land-based bombers, the Port Moresby invasion force turned back to Rabaul.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Acting on intelligence, the Allies committed their carriers to meet the Japanese advance. Both sides made many mistakes in the new kind of fighting; the Naval History and Heritage Command quotes Samuel Eliot Morison calling it a battle of errors in which the enemy made more and failed to profit by them. The Japanese decision to turn back the invasion force, once their air groups were too battered to cover it, decided the outcome.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The heavy losses of Japanese aircraft and the damage to Shōkaku left the Japanese unable to cover the landing at Port Moresby, and the invasion was called off.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Japanese sank more ships, and the Naval History and Heritage Command calls the battle a Japanese tactical victory. But Port Moresby remained in Allied hands, and Britannica calls the battle a strategic Allied victory. It was the first time since Pearl Harbor that the Japanese advance had been checked.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Shōkaku was too badly damaged to join the force for Midway, and Zuikaku, having lost pilots and aircraft, did not take part either; Coral Sea reduced the carriers available to Japan for Midway by a third. It was the first naval battle in which the ships never sighted or fired at each other, and it foreshadowed the carrier warfare of the rest of the Pacific War.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A tactical draw, or even a tactical defeat, can be a strategic victory if it stops the enemy's purpose. Intelligence that reveals the enemy's objective allows a weaker force to be in the right place. In carrier warfare, reconnaissance under uncertainty decides who strikes first and at what.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources judge the outcome differently: the Naval History and Heritage Command calls it a Japanese tactical victory that nonetheless stopped the advance, Britannica a strategic Allied victory. The Naval History and Heritage Command dates the operations from 29 April, Britannica and the Australian War Memorial the battle from 4 May.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Naval History and Heritage Command gives the Japanese plan, the air strikes, the losses and the battle's effect on Midway. Britannica gives the intelligence, the course of the battle and its strategic result. The Australian War Memorial gives the Allied forces, including the Australian cruisers, and the turning back of the invasion force.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Pearl Harbor Japan occupied islands across the western Pacific as a defensive buffer. The victories at the Coral Sea and Midway in the spring of 1942 meant that the Japanese navy could no longer mount major offensives, and the Allies could begin their own. In July 1942 Japanese troops and labourers began building an airfield on Guadalcanal in the southern Solomons.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Aircraft based on the new airfield would threaten Allied bases in the New Hebrides and New Caledonia, Port Moresby and the supply routes to Australia and New Zealand. The Allies took immediate steps to eject the Japanese with the forces available in the South Pacific.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Allies aimed to seize the airfield on Guadalcanal and the harbour at Tulagi and hold them. The Japanese aimed to retake the airfield, reinforcing the island by sea and bombarding the field, and to defeat the American naval forces that supported it.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Guadalcanal is a jungle-covered island in the southern Solomons. The airfield, renamed Henderson Field, lay at Lunga Point; across the sound lay Florida Island and Tulagi. Rabaul, the main Japanese base in the region, lay some 1,050 kilometres to the north-west, while aircraft at Henderson Field could strike ships in the surrounding waters. The jungle, the weather and the lack of infrastructure made supply and movement extremely difficult.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The 1st Marine Division under Major General Alexander Vandegrift made the landing, supported by naval task forces; it was later reinforced and in December relieved by US Army divisions. Vice Admiral Robert Ghormley commanded the naval forces in the South Pacific until Vice Admiral William Halsey succeeded him on 18 October. The aircraft at Henderson Field, the “Cactus Air Force”, combined Marine, Navy and Army aviators. On the Japanese side, the Seventeenth Army fought on the island, supported by the fleet; Rear Admiral Tanaka Raizō's destroyers ran the night reinforcement convoys known as the Tokyo Express.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 7–8 August 1942 the Marines landed on Guadalcanal, Tulagi and neighbouring islands in the US Navy's first offensive amphibious operation in the Pacific. They met little resistance on Guadalcanal and took the almost complete airfield within about a day and a half, while the Japanese defenders of Tulagi fought almost to the last man. Vandegrift formed a tight perimeter around Henderson Field.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On the night of 8–9 August Japanese cruisers surprised the Allied screening force off Savo Island, sank three American cruisers and crippled an Australian one, the worst defeat in a single fleet action suffered by the US Navy. The Japanese then counterattacked on land, at the Tenaru in August and at Edson's Ridge on 13–14 September, and at sea, in the carrier battle of the Eastern Solomons on 24 August. Cape Esperance on 11–12 October and the carrier battle of Santa Cruz on 26 October, a Japanese tactical victory that cost them heavily in aircrew, accompanied a major Japanese ground offensive against the Henderson perimeter on 23–26 October, which failed. In the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal on 12–15 November the US Navy blocked Japan's last major attempt to retake the island from the sea. From then on American reinforcements outpaced Japanese ones, and at the end of December the Japanese high command accepted the case for evacuation, which began in late January; the last troops were taken off by destroyers on the night of 7 February 1943.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Vandegrift's decision to concentrate his Marines in a tight perimeter around the airfield kept the key to the campaign in American hands, and warning from code-breakers helped him meet the first attacks. Japanese commanders, believing after Savo Island that most Americans had withdrawn, underestimated the garrison. Halsey concentrated his carriers for Santa Cruz, and in November the US Navy accepted heavy losses in night actions to stop the reinforcement convoys.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The repulse of the October ground offensive and the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal in November decided the campaign: after November the Japanese could no longer seriously threaten Henderson Field, and the Tokyo Express could no longer operate with impunity. A Japanese officer reportedly called the November battle the fork in the road.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Guadalcanal was in Allied hands by February 1943, and the American positions in the southern Solomons were never again seriously threatened. Both sides lost many ships in the waters off the island, which became known as Ironbottom Sound; the Japanese also lost aircraft and experienced aircrew they could not replace.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Together with Midway, the Naval History and Heritage Command judges, the victory on Guadalcanal was probably the turning point of the Pacific War, and Japan was now on the defensive. It was the first step in the Allied advance that went on through the Gilbert, Marshall and Mariana Islands to Iwo Jima and Okinawa. American troops suffered heavily from malaria and other tropical diseases, and the Japanese troops on the island were weakened as their supply failed.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An island base is only as strong as its air cover and the ability to supply it; whoever could reinforce faster would hold Guadalcanal. In a campaign of attrition the stronger industrial power gains by accepting battle repeatedly, as long as it holds the key position. Intelligence, surface night-fighting skill and the use of a single airfield shaped the outcome as much as any one battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the end differently: the Naval History and Heritage Command gives the last evacuation on the night of 7 February, Britannica the elimination of the last pocket on 8 February. They also give different totals for losses on both sides. The National WWII Museum stresses early American mistakes in moving supplies inland, while Britannica stresses the success of the initial landing.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the naval and land campaigns in detail, from the landings to the evacuation. The National WWII Museum gives the strategic setting, the October offensive and the campaign's significance. The Naval History and Heritage Command gives the naval battles, the Japanese decision to evacuate and its judgment of the campaign.

H-019-4: “Black May”: Battle of the Atlantic 1943 (Samuel J. Cox)
Battle of the Atlantic (Thomas A. Hughes and Marc Milner)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Britain depended on supplies from North America and the Empire carried across the Atlantic in merchant ships, which German submarines (U-boats) and surface warships could attack. The first Atlantic convoy sailed on 2 September 1939. After the fall of France in June 1940 the U-boats gained bases on the French Atlantic coast, and Churchill coined the name the Battle of the Atlantic in March 1941.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: For the Allies the battle meant blockading the Axis, securing their own sea movements and being able to project military power across the ocean; Churchill saw it as Germany's best chance to defeat the Western powers. Any invasion of Europe depended on carrying troops and supplies across the Atlantic. When the United States entered the war, U-boats sank many unescorted ships off its east coast in early 1942 until convoys were introduced.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Grand Admiral Karl Dönitz, commander of the U-boat arm and later of the whole German navy, aimed to frustrate the Allied use of the Atlantic by sinking merchant shipping. The Allies aimed to deliver their convoys safely and, increasingly, to destroy the U-boats attacking them.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Atlantic covers more than 100 million square kilometres, so that a convoy was hard to find. In the mid-Atlantic, beyond the reach of most land-based aircraft, lay the air gap where convoys had no air cover and were most vulnerable. U-boats returning to the French bases had to cross the Bay of Biscay.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Allies grouped merchant ships into convoys escorted by warships and, where possible, aircraft; British, Canadian and, from 1941, American navies and air forces shared the escort of the North Atlantic. Dönitz directed his U-boats by radio from his headquarters, assembling them into groups, the wolf packs, on patrol lines across the convoy routes. Both sides fought a war of intelligence: German code-breakers read British convoy codes from 1941 into 1943, while the British read naval Enigma traffic until a fourth rotor was added in February 1942.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: By May 1941 a fully escorted transatlantic convoy system was in place, and the loss of the battleship Bismarck that month ended German surface raids. The expansion of convoys in the western hemisphere forced the U-boats back into the mid-Atlantic by late 1942, where the battle reached its climax.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The crisis peaked in March 1943, when the Allies again lost the ability to read U-boat signals for a time and U-boats sank great numbers of ships in a few weeks. By then decisions of the Casablanca Conference had begun to push naval and air reinforcements into the North Atlantic. In April and May improving weather, very-long-range Liberator aircraft that closed the air gap, escort carriers, roving support groups, centimetric radar, high-frequency direction-finding and new weapons such as the Hedgehog and an air-dropped homing torpedo came together. In early May the escorts of convoy ONS-5 beat off repeated attacks. U-boat losses became unsustainable, and on 24 May Dönitz withdrew his U-boats from the North Atlantic. Renewed attacks with acoustic torpedoes in the autumn failed, and for the rest of the war the Allies controlled the Atlantic sea-lanes.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Allied decision to give anti-submarine production top priority, and the decisions at Casablanca to reinforce the North Atlantic, provided the ships, aircraft and escort carriers that turned the battle. Dönitz's central control of the wolf packs by radio, which the Germans believed secure, exposed them to direction-finding even when their codes could not be read. His recall order of 24 May accepted that his losses were no longer matched by sinkings.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: May 1943, known as Black May, was the turning point: U-boat losses rose sharply while sinkings fell. The Naval History and Heritage Command notes that by then American shipyards were producing far more ships than the Germans could sink, while the Germans were losing more submarines than they could replace.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The U-boats never regained the initiative and were almost constantly on the defensive from the autumn of 1943. Shipping losses fell sharply, and supplies and troops crossed to Britain for the invasion of 1944.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Atlantic was the longest campaign of the war, from September 1939 to May 1945. Victory there, with the opening of the Mediterranean to through traffic, brought significant reductions in shipping losses and allowed the build-up for the invasion of Normandy. The Naval History and Heritage Command also notes the importance of the Arctic convoys to the Soviet Union, which came at a critical time.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Success in a campaign against shipping is measured in ships delivered and ships built, not only in submarines sunk. Technology, intelligence, numbers and tactics improved by experience and scientific analysis combined to turn the battle; none alone was decisive. A side that believes its communications secure may expose itself in ways it does not suspect.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The relative weight of code-breaking against technology, air power and industry is debated. The Naval History and Heritage Command argues that no single factor was decisive and that Allied intelligence against the U-boats was at its weakest during the turning point of May 1943; Britannica lists the repenetration of the U-boat codes among the causes of the May defeat. The Naval History and Heritage Command also warns that statistics for the battle should be treated with caution because sources count them differently.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Imperial War Museums give the convoy system and the course of the battle to May 1943. Samuel J. Cox's account for the Naval History and Heritage Command gives the intelligence war, the technologies, the production race and Dönitz's withdrawal. Thomas A. Hughes and Marc Milner's Britannica article gives the phases of the whole battle and its strategic importance.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Pearl Harbor Japan invaded Burma, and Rangoon fell by March 1942. British and Indian forces made a fighting retreat of about 1,600 kilometres into India, the longest in British history. In November 1943 South East Asia Command was formed under Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Earlier in the war British troops had fallen back when their supply lines were cut and had largely stopped operations in the monsoon. South East Asia Command now ordered troops to stand firm, rely on air supply and keep fighting. The Japanese sought to pre-empt a planned British invasion of Burma.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: In March 1944 the Japanese Fifteenth Army launched Operation U-Go to capture the British supply bases on the Imphal Plain and cut the Dimapur–Imphal road at Kohima. Holding Imphal would disrupt Allied air supplies to China, delay a British return to Burma and give Japan a base for attacks on India.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Imphal, capital of Manipur, lay on a plain ringed by hills and was the main British base in the region. Kohima, a small village on a ridge on the road from Dimapur, controlled the route by which Imphal could be relieved. The monsoon began during the battle.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Lieutenant-General Renya Mutaguchi commanded three Japanese divisions and one Indian National Army division. Lieutenant-General William Slim's Fourteenth Army held the front: IV Corps under Geoffrey Scoones at Imphal, and XXXIII Corps under Montagu Stopford, which relieved Kohima and Imphal. Slim had rebuilt the army's morale, trained it in jungle warfare and introduced defensive boxes that could be supplied by air.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Mutaguchi expected to destroy IV Corps quickly and seize its supplies before his own logistics failed. The 33rd Division was to cut off the 17th Indian Division south of Imphal and the 15th Division to cut the road to Kohima, while the 31st Division under Kotoku Sato surrounded Kohima to block relief from Dimapur. The defenders of Kohima were a scratch garrison under Colonel Hugh Richards.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Japanese attack on Imphal began in early March, and on 29 March they cut the Imphal–Kohima road. By early April both Kohima and Imphal were surrounded. At Kohima the garrison, supplied by air, held a shrinking perimeter on Garrison Hill from 5 to 18 April in some of the bitterest fighting of the war, at one point separated from the Japanese only by the tennis court of the Deputy Commissioner's bungalow; the British 2nd Division broke through on 18 April. Fighting around Kohima went on until mid-May, when Sato's division began to withdraw. Japanese attacks on Imphal failed against the Indian divisions there. Despite the monsoon, the Allies counter-attacked up the road, and on 22 June XXXIII Corps linked up with IV Corps at Imphal. The battles ended on 18 July.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Slim's army stood and fought on the Imphal plain, its encircled formations supplied by air rather than retreating, as South East Asia Command now required. Mountbatten sent the 2nd Division to Dimapur, and the 5th Indian Division was flown from the Arakan to Imphal in two days. Mutaguchi gambled on capturing Allied supplies, quarrelled with his divisional commanders and kept attacking long after the offensive had clearly failed, when he could have withdrawn.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The garrison's stand at Kohima and the failure of the attacks on Imphal by early May denied the Japanese the supplies they depended on. Allied logistics and air supply, which the National Army Museum calls decisive, allowed rapid reinforcement and kept the garrisons fighting.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The National Army Museum calls Imphal–Kohima one of the biggest defeats the Japanese army ever suffered. When Mutaguchi's plan to seize Allied supplies failed, his men starved during the worst of the monsoon; most of his army was killed, wounded or missing. Mutaguchi was relieved of command and forced into retirement.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory opened the way for the reconquest of Burma. The Fourteenth Army crossed the Chindwin during the monsoon, supplied by air, won bridgeheads over the Irrawaddy and took Meiktila and Mandalay in March 1945, and Rangoon fell in May. The cemeteries at Imphal and Kohima, with the Kohima Epitaph, commemorate the dead.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Logistics decided the battle: an offensive that depends on capturing the enemy's supplies fails if the enemy holds, while air supply allowed encircled troops to stand. Morale, training and confidence restored by a commander can turn a defeated army into a winning one. Persisting with a failed offensive turns a setback into a disaster.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources give different loss figures. Both the National Army Museum and the Imperial War Museums call the battle a turning point, but the Imperial War Museums note that it is among the lesser-known battles of the war. The role of the Indian National Army is mentioned in the sources read only as one division under Mutaguchi.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the background, the commanders, the plans, the sieges, the air supply and the aftermath, and in a separate article Slim's methods. The Imperial War Museums give Operation U-Go, the siege of Kohima, the link-up and the outcome.

sources.title: Operation Bagration: The Greatest Military Defeat Of All Time? (Helen Upcraft, video and transcript)
Eastern Front: Russian advance to the Vistula (summer 1944) (Basil Liddell Hart)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the spring of 1944 the tide on the Eastern Front had turned, and German strength was in irreversible decline. Soviet officers had developed a doctrine of deep battle: successive breakthroughs at several points, through which mobile forces would drive into the enemy's rear and destroy his ability to fight. The Red Army aimed to inflict on the Germans a catastrophe on the scale of Barbarossa.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Western Allies were about to land in France, and Bagration was launched in support of the Normandy invasion. Hitler wanted to hold as much territory in the east as possible until the landings in the west had been defeated, and Army Group Centre, holding a great salient in Belorussia, was forbidden to retreat.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Soviet plan, named by Stalin after Prince Pyotr Bagration, who fell at Borodino in 1812, was a succession of attacks by four fronts to encircle and destroy the German forces in the Belorussian salient and open the way to the pre-war Soviet border. Stalin gave his commanders more autonomy than in earlier offensives.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Belorussian salient lay north of the Pripet Marshes, the best-fortified sector of the German front, with Vitebsk, Orsha, Mogilev and Bobruisk forward and Minsk behind. German communications were long and exposed to partisans; Soviet communications were shorter. The marshes were believed impassable to heavy vehicles.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Field Marshal Ernst Busch's Army Group Centre consisted of experienced units, but German intelligence expected the Soviet summer offensive further south, against Walter Model's Army Group North Ukraine, and most German armour had been moved there. Four Soviet fronts were massed against Army Group Centre with a large advantage in men, artillery and tanks, and near-total control of the air; Konstantin Rokossovsky's armies formed the southern wing, north of the Pripet Marshes. Large partisan forces operated in the German rear.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: A deception campaign, maskirovka, disguised the Soviet build-up: civilians were moved from the front, camouflage was checked from the air and strict radio silence enforced. On the night of 19 June partisans detonated demolition charges across the railways and bridges in the German rear, hampering reinforcement. When German commanders sought to move to a more flexible defence, Busch refused.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Bagration began on 22 June, three years to the day after the German invasion. Attacks near Vitebsk on 22 June were followed on 23 June by attacks toward Orsha and Mogilev and on 24 June toward Bobruisk, behind massive barrages. Vitebsk was encircled by 24 June and Bobruisk on 27 June, where Rokossovsky's armies broke through north of the marshes. Hitler designated towns as fortified places to be held to the last man; many were bypassed and cut off. He replaced Busch with Model on 28 June, but Minsk fell on 3 July and a large German force was trapped east of it. The Soviets advanced into Lithuania and Poland, other offensives joined in, and on 31 July one of Rokossovsky's columns reached the suburbs of Warsaw. By the first week of August the advance was halted by exhausted supply lines.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Soviet command's choice of the Belorussian salient, its deception and its readiness to shift exploitation to wherever breakthroughs succeeded, as when the 5th Guards Tank Army moved north to Vitebsk after Orsha held, turned breakthroughs into encirclements. Hitler's refusal to allow withdrawal and his fortified-place orders left German forces to be surrounded. American trucks supplied under Lend-Lease let the Soviet mobile forces move and be supplied deep in the German rear.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The encirclements at Vitebsk and Bobruisk in the first week and the fall of Minsk on 3 July, with a large German force trapped east of it, broke Army Group Centre; the IWM notes that in a few weeks it effectively ceased to exist.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Army Group Centre was destroyed, with close to 30 divisions lost, and Belorussia was liberated before the end of July. The Red Army advanced as much as 724 kilometres in five weeks, the longest and fastest advance it had yet made, reaching the Vistula and pressing deep into Lithuania. Both sides suffered very heavy losses.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: As the Red Army advanced it found mass graves of murdered civilians and razed towns and villages left by the German occupation. German prisoners were paraded through Moscow on 17 July, and many died in Soviet labour camps. When the Polish Home Army rose in Warsaw on 1 August, the Red Army halted across the Vistula and gave no support; the Germans crushed the uprising, killed very large numbers of civilians and razed the city, a result that, Britannica notes, served Soviet purposes in Poland. With Overlord in the west, Bagration put the Allies in a position to crush Germany from east and west.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Deep operations, multiple breakthroughs followed by rapid exploitation, could destroy an army group when combined with deception and mobility. Rigid holding orders help the attacker by leaving the defender to be encircled. An advance is limited in the end by its logistics.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the start to 22 June (Imperial War Museums) or 23 June (Britannica) and give different figures for German and Soviet losses. The Imperial War Museums argue that the operation is less well known in the West than D-Day because of the Western focus on British and American operations and the Cold War. Britannica judges the halt before Warsaw intentional, while the Imperial War Museums also stress Soviet exhaustion after a 700-kilometre advance.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Normandy landings and the pursuit of the German armies across France and Belgium in the summer of 1944, the Allies sought the fastest way to win the war in Europe. Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery believed that one bold stroke could shorten the war.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Montgomery persuaded the Supreme Allied Commander, General Dwight D. Eisenhower, to approve a combined airborne and armoured assault through the Netherlands and to divert supplies, especially scarce fuel, to support it.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Three airborne divisions, the US 101st and 82nd and the British 1st, were to seize the bridges along a single road through Eindhoven, Nijmegen and Arnhem (Operation Market), while XXX Corps advanced along it to cross the Rhine (Operation Garden). Success would outflank the Siegfried Line, liberate the Netherlands and open the way to the Ruhr.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The bridge at Arnhem, the farthest objective, lay about 100 kilometres from XXX Corps' start line. XXX Corps had to advance along a single narrow causeway, vulnerable to traffic jams and counter-attack, with marshes preventing movement off the road in places. Around Arnhem the wooded ground cut the range of the airborne radios.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The First Allied Airborne Army's three divisions, joined at Arnhem by the 1st Independent Polish Parachute Brigade, were lightly armed, with few heavy weapons against tanks. Major-General Roy Urquhart commanded the British 1st Airborne Division. Opposing them was Field Marshal Walter Model's Army Group B; intelligence had indicated that the area was lightly defended, but elements of two SS armoured divisions were present.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: There were too few transport aircraft to fly all the airborne troops in at once, so they were landed in three lifts, one a day. The British landing zones were about 10 kilometres west of the Arnhem bridge.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 17 September the airborne divisions landed. The 101st took most of its bridges near Eindhoven within hours, and the 82nd landed near Nijmegen. At Arnhem only the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Parachute Brigade reached the bridge and held its north end; the other battalions fought into Arnhem with heavy losses but never reached it, and the rest of the division was pressed into a pocket at Oosterbeek. XXX Corps, delayed by German defenders and blown bridges, linked up with the 82nd, and the Nijmegen bridge was taken, but the tanks did not move on for 18 hours. The battalion at the Arnhem bridge was overrun. The Polish brigade landed late and could not help, fog and low cloud hampered resupply, and German counter-attacks cut the corridor. On the night of 24–25 September the survivors of the 1st Airborne Division were ferried back across the Rhine.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Eisenhower's decision to back Montgomery's plan concentrated scarce resources on a single narrow thrust. The planners accepted landing zones far from the Arnhem bridge, a lift spread over three days and an intelligence picture of a lightly defended area. Model reacted quickly, calling for reinforcements and air support and blowing bridges along the road.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The failure to take the Arnhem bridge in strength on the first day, and XXX Corps' delays on the single road, especially at Nijmegen, decided the operation: XXX Corps could not reach Arnhem before German forces overwhelmed the British defenders.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The operation failed. All the bridges except Arnhem were captured, but most of the 1st Airborne Division was killed or captured, and the IWM records that only about a fifth of the men who dropped at Arnhem made it back.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Rhine crossing and the capture of the Ruhr were delayed by six months, and the Allies had to fight into Germany on a broad front. The operation did liberate a large part of the Netherlands, at a time when many Dutch people were close to starvation.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A plan that depends on everything going right along a single road has no margin for delay. Intelligence that contradicts a plan's optimistic assumptions must be weighed rather than discounted. Airborne troops can seize objectives but cannot hold them for long against armour without relief.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica calls the operation a failure of military intelligence redeemed to some extent by the heroism of the soldiers; the National Army Museum calls it a costly failure but a remarkable feat of arms, and the IWM one of the most controversial episodes of the war. The sources give different dates for the end of the operation, 25 or 27 September, and different loss figures.

sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the plan, the problems of landing zones, radios, weather and intelligence, and the outcome. Raymond K. Bluhm's Britannica article gives Montgomery's persuasion of Eisenhower, the course of the battle at each bridge and Model's response. The Imperial War Museums give Montgomery's aims and the fate of the airborne troops at Arnhem.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the autumn of 1944 the Japanese had been driven from many outposts in the south-west and central Pacific, and American and British naval power had grown enormously. The Allied offensive of 1944 was to culminate in an invasion of the Philippines.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The invasion aimed to cut Japan's supply lines to the East Indies and win bases for further operations. King, Nimitz and Marshall had favoured other routes, but General Douglas MacArthur, determined to return to the Philippines, prevailed. The assault on Leyte joined the central Pacific advance under Admiral Chester Nimitz and the south-west Pacific advance under MacArthur.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Japanese responded with Sho-Go, the Victory Operation: a decoy force of carriers would draw Admiral William Halsey's Third Fleet north, while three surface forces converged on Leyte Gulf to destroy the landing. Kurita told his interrogators in 1945 that his mission was to destroy the landing forces at daybreak on 25 October; Ozawa said the decoy was basically Admiral Toyoda's idea and that he expected his fleet to be destroyed. The Americans aimed to protect the landing and, in Halsey's orders, to destroy the major part of the Japanese fleet if the chance arose.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Leyte, in the central Philippines, had an undefended approach from the east and good anchorages. The Japanese central force had to pass through the Sibuyan Sea and the San Bernardino Strait north of Samar; the southern forces through the Surigao Strait. The battle was fought in several widely separated engagements.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: MacArthur had overall command of the Leyte operation; Vice Admiral Thomas Kinkaid's Seventh Fleet, his principal naval force, supported the landings, while Halsey's Third Fleet, with the fast carriers and battleships, reported to Nimitz. No single commander controlled both fleets. On the Japanese side Vice Admiral Kurita Takeo led the central force with the battleships Yamato and Musashi, Vice Admirals Nishimura Shōji and Shima Kiyohide the southern forces, and Vice Admiral Ozawa Jisaburō the decoy carriers, which had few aircraft: Ozawa said many of his carrier aircraft had been sent to Formosa on Toyoda's orders. The Japanese forces were coordinated only through Toyoda, by radio.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 20 October American troops landed on the east coast of Leyte almost unopposed, and MacArthur waded ashore. The Japanese had chosen to defend farther inland. Their fleet was already moving under Sho-Go.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 23 October American submarines found Kurita's force off Palawan and sank two heavy cruisers, including his flagship. On 24 October Third Fleet aircraft sank the battleship Musashi in the Sibuyan Sea, while a Japanese bomb set the light carrier Princeton ablaze; Kurita turned west, then resumed his course. That night Nishimura's force was annihilated in the Surigao Strait by the battleships and cruisers of the Seventh Fleet and an Australian task force, and Shima turned back. Halsey, sighting Ozawa's carriers, took the whole Third Fleet north. At dawn on 25 October Kurita's battleships came out of the San Bernardino Strait off Samar and met Taffy 3, a group of escort carriers, destroyers and destroyer escorts, which fought back so fiercely, with aircraft from other task groups, that Kurita broke off and withdrew. Off Cape Engaño Halsey's aircraft sank all four of Ozawa's carriers. On 25 October the first kamikaze attack sank an escort carrier.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Halsey's decision to take the whole Third Fleet north after Ozawa's decoy, without leaving a force to guard the San Bernardino Strait, left the landing area exposed; Nimitz's signal asking where Task Force 34 was, with its padding misread as a rebuke, finally turned him back. Kurita's decision to withdraw off Samar, when he was close to the transports, saved the Seventh Fleet. Kurita told his interrogators that he expected heavy air attack inside the Gulf and judged that he could do no good there, so he turned north to join Ozawa against the American carriers; fuel, he said, was no consideration in that choice, though it governed his later withdrawal. Ozawa accepted that his force was meant to be sacrificed; he had little confidence in the lure and put its chances at even.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The destruction of the southern force at Surigao Strait, the resistance of Taffy 3 off Samar and Kurita's withdrawal decided the battle: Sho-Go failed to reach the landing area. Japanese communications failed at the decisive moment: according to an officer from Ozawa's flagship, questioned with Kurita, the reports Ozawa sent on 24 October never reached Kurita, who therefore did not know that the decoy had worked, while Ozawa believed it was failing.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Sho-Go failed to disrupt the Leyte landings and cost Japan most of what remained of its fleet, including four carriers and the battleship Musashi. The National WWII Museum calls the result a decisive American victory that ended the Japanese navy as a strategic force; Britannica writes that it crippled the Combined Fleet and reinforced Allied control of the Pacific.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: MacArthur's campaign went on to Luzon and Manila, and the way opened to Okinawa. Organised kamikaze attacks, first met off Samar, killed thousands of Allied personnel in the remaining months of the war.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Divided command over forces fighting the same battle invites failure; at Leyte the lack of a single commander over Halsey and Kinkaid nearly cost the landing. Ambiguous orders and signals shape decisions as much as the enemy does. A fleet without air cover is helpless, as Samuel Eliot Morison concluded from the battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Halsey's decision has been debated from the moment it was made; the National WWII Museum lists his ambiguous orders, his wish to sink carriers, his belief that Kurita was retreating and poor intelligence on Japanese air losses. Kurita's reasons for withdrawing are also disputed: he may have taken the escort carriers for fleet carriers, could not know that the decoy had worked, and later said he feared air attack in the gulf; some officers called him a coward. His own account, given to American interrogators in October 1945, stresses the air threat and his judgment that he could not be effective in the Gulf, and plays down fuel; it should be read as testimony given to the victors after the war.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the strategic setting, the landings, Sho-Go and each engagement in detail, with Nimitz's signal and its aftermath. The National WWII Museum gives the command arrangements, the Japanese plan, the course of the battle and the debates over Halsey's and Kurita's decisions. The U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey's interrogations of Kurita and Ozawa in Tokyo in October 1945 give the two Japanese commanders' own accounts of their missions and decisions.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the breakout from Normandy the Allies crossed France into Belgium, but their advance lost momentum in the autumn of 1944, apart from the failed thrust to Arnhem. Some Allied leaders predicted that the war would end by Christmas, while the German defence was strengthened with reserves and new forces.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Hitler saw a last chance in the west. He hoped a decisive blow would split the Western Allies and lead to a negotiated peace that would let him concentrate on the Eastern Front.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The German offensive was to break through the American front in the Ardennes, cross the Meuse and drive to Antwerp, cutting off the British army group from the Americans and from its supplies. The Fifth Panzer Army was to wheel north-west past Namur to Antwerp, and the Sixth Panzer Army to thrust past Liège.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Ardennes in Belgium and Luxembourg is hilly and wooded country, regarded as difficult for a large offensive. The woods concealed the German concentration, but deep valleys turned the through roads into bottlenecks, which made road junctions such as St Vith and Bastogne vital. Winter weather at first grounded Allied aircraft.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt had overall command of the offensive; the Fifth Panzer Army was led by Hasso von Manteuffel and the Sixth Panzer Army by Sepp Dietrich. General Dwight D. Eisenhower, the Supreme Allied Commander, held a front of nearly 1,000 kilometres; in the Ardennes the Allied troops were mainly American, some new and inexperienced, others exhausted.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Germans massed their forces in secret, moving at night and under radio silence, and timed the attack for weather that would keep Allied aircraft on the ground.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The offensive began before dawn on 16 December 1944 and achieved complete surprise, pushing a bulge into the American line. Small American units delayed the spearhead, and on 17 December soldiers of Kampfgruppe Peiper murdered American prisoners near Malmedy. The defenders of St Vith held the crossroads for nearly a week, and Bastogne, surrounded, was held by the 101st Airborne Division; on 22 December its commander, Anthony McAuliffe, answered a demand for surrender with “NUTS!”. By 24 December the Fifth Panzer Army was within about 6 kilometres of the Meuse, but fuel shortages and growing air attacks stopped it. Patton's Third Army relieved Bastogne on 26 December. The weather cleared and Allied air attacks resumed; on 1 January the Luftwaffe struck Allied airfields but suffered losses it could not recover from. The First Army counter-attacked on 3 January, and by the end of January the Allies had regained their former positions.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Montgomery, who took charge on the northern flank, swung his reserves south to forestall the Germans at the Meuse crossings, and Patton's Third Army broke through to relieve Bastogne. The quick arrival of Allied reinforcements and the decision to hold the road junctions at St Vith and Bastogne, even when surrounded, slowed the German advance. The Germans then carried out a skilful withdrawal from the potential trap.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The stands at St Vith, Bastogne and on the northern shoulder denied the Germans the roads they needed, and by the end of December, short of fuel and under renewed air attack, their advance had ground to a halt.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Allied line bulged but did not break. Germany lost men and material it could not replace, and Britannica judges that while the offensive upset Allied preparations, it forfeited any chance of prolonged German resistance. Churchill called it undoubtedly the greatest American battle of the war, and it was one of the bloodiest.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Germany had drained its last reserves of manpower and material in the west. The Allies resumed their advance and in early spring crossed into the heart of Germany. The murder of American prisoners near Malmedy was one of the most brutal war crimes against American troops in Europe.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Complacency and confidence that the enemy is beaten invite surprise. Holding road junctions in difficult country can stop an offensive that depends on speed and captured fuel. Rapid regrouping of reserves and decisive commanders turned a crisis into a defeat for the attacker.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the end of the battle to 16 January (Britannica) or 25 January 1945 (the National WWII Museum, the IWM). Britannica credits Montgomery's swing of reserves to the Meuse with frustrating the German advance; the brief's controversy over his press conference is not discussed in the sources read. Britannica judges the offensive profitable in its own terms but fatal in relation to the whole war.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the German plan, the commanders, the course of the battle and its assessment. The National WWII Museum gives Hitler's aims, the German preparations, the delaying actions, the Malmedy massacre and the defence of St Vith and Bastogne. The IWM gives the surprise, the role of the road junctions, the weather and fuel, and the outcome.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The American counteroffensive in the Pacific was divided between MacArthur, advancing through New Guinea to the Philippines, and Admiral Chester Nimitz, advancing across the central Pacific. By October 1944 MacArthur had landed in the Philippines and Nimitz had taken the Mariana Islands, from which B-29 bombers could strike Japan.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: General Henry Arnold of the Army Air Forces wanted Iwo Jima, halfway between the Marianas and Tokyo, as a base for fighters to escort the bombers. Nimitz, on his admirals' advice, proposed taking Iwo Jima and Okinawa rather than Formosa, and the Joint Chiefs approved. The island was part of the Tokyo prefecture, Japanese home soil.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Operation Detachment aimed to take the island and its airfields. The Japanese aimed to inflict such heavy losses that the Americans might be deterred from invading the home islands.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Iwo Jima is a small volcanic island, about 8 kilometres long, about 1,220 kilometres from Tokyo, dotted with caves and covered with volcanic sand and ash. Mount Suribachi, at its south-western tip, overlooks most of the island; two airfields lay in the middle and a third, unfinished, to the north. The landing beaches were backed by steep terraces of volcanic ash.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Lieutenant General Kuribayashi Tadamichi, sent in May 1944 to organise the defence, had his garrison build a network of tunnels and hundreds of pillboxes, blockhouses and gun positions. Rather than defend the beaches heavily, he kept his men underground until the Americans had advanced inland, and ordered them not to make banzai charges. Nimitz formed a joint expeditionary force; Major General Harry Schmidt led the Marine landing force of three Marine divisions. US intelligence underestimated the garrison.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Marines' commander asked for ten days of naval bombardment but was given three because of the schedule for Okinawa; poor weather and the buried defences meant it did little damage. The Marines were to land on the south-eastern beaches, cut across the island to isolate Suribachi and drive north past the airfields.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: At about 9 a.m. on 19 February 1945 the Marines landed. The ash terraces slowed them and the beaches became congested under Japanese fire, but by evening Suribachi was cut off. On 21 February kamikaze aircraft damaged several American ships. Marines took Suribachi on 23 February and twice raised a flag on its summit; Joe Rosenthal's photograph of the second raising became one of the war's most famous images. The Marines then fought north yard by yard, taking the airfields and fighting for weeks at places they called the Meat Grinder and the Amphitheater, using flamethrowers against caves and bunkers. On 8 March a Japanese naval officer led a banzai attack against Kuribayashi's orders. The island was declared secure on 16 March, but the last major engagement was a night attack on 26 March.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Kuribayashi's decision to give up the beaches and fight from tunnels and caves, and to forbid banzai charges, made the Marines pay for every position. On the American side, the decision to shorten the bombardment to keep to the Okinawa schedule, and an underestimate of the garrison, made the landing costlier.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The capture of Suribachi on 23 February and the breakthrough of the central Japanese line at the end of February decided the battle, but the defenders fought on in the north for weeks.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The United States took Iwo Jima at a cost among the heaviest in the history of the Marine Corps. Almost the entire Japanese garrison was killed; only a few hundred were taken prisoner, and Kuribayashi himself did not surrender. Twenty-seven Medals of Honor were awarded, fourteen of them posthumously.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The island's airfields were used for the rest of the war, and B-29s landed there. The National WWII Museum notes that the bloodbath horrified Allied planners and the public, who feared an even greater slaughter in an invasion of Japan. The flag-raising photograph became a symbol, reproduced on posters and a stamp and in the Marine Corps War Memorial.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A defence in depth, dug in against overwhelming firepower, can make the cost of an objective very high even when defeat is certain. An objective's value must be weighed against that cost before the attack, not justified afterwards.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Whether the island was worth its cost is debated. Britannica cites the historian Robert Burrell's finding that the fighter escort missions that were the main reason for the invasion were few, that most B-29 landings were not strictly emergencies, and that the Joint Chiefs did not consider the Marines' doubts. The sources date the end of the battle to 16 or 26 March. The National WWII Museum describes the long confusion over whether the flag-raising photograph was staged.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Myles Hudson's Britannica article gives the strategic background, Kuribayashi's defence, the course of the battle and the debate over its cost. The National WWII Museum's article on Iwo Jima and Okinawa gives the defence and the fighting, and Keith Huxen's 75th-anniversary article gives the flag-raising and its legacy.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: As the battle for Iwo Jima ended in March 1945, American commanders prepared Operation Iceberg, the invasion of Okinawa. American planners expected the losses of Iwo Jima to be repeated on a much greater scale, and hoped to overwhelm the defenders with a massive bombardment and the largest amphibious landing of the Pacific War.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Okinawa, the largest of the Ryukyu Islands, lies about 563 kilometres south of Kyushu, and its capture was regarded as a vital precursor to a ground invasion of the Japanese home islands. It was the last island battle before that anticipated invasion.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Americans aimed to take the island as a springboard for the invasion of Japan. The Japanese aimed to make the cost as high as possible, on land from prepared positions in the south and at sea with mass suicide attacks on the fleet.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Okinawa is about 100 kilometres long and at most 32 kilometres wide. Its southern part, around Naha and Shuri, was heavily fortified along high ridges, with Shuri Castle as the keystone, and its many caves gave the defenders shelter from bombardment. The island had a large civilian population, which the Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum describes as fully mobilized for the battle, the only ground battle fought on Japanese soil. Heavy rain and rugged terrain slowed the fighting.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Under the overall command of Admiral Chester Nimitz, Admiral Raymond Spruance's Fifth Fleet oversaw the landings and Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. commanded the US Tenth Army of Army and Marine divisions. Lieutenant General Ushijima Mitsuru commanded the Japanese garrison, which had thoroughly fortified the island. Japan retained enough aircraft for mass suicide attacks.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Air and sea attacks began as early as October 1944, and in March 1945 the carriers of Task Force 58 destroyed hundreds of Japanese aircraft. On 26 March American troops landed on the Kerama Islands to the west, where they found boats assembled for suicide attacks, and artillery was placed on the islets of Keise to support the main landing.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 1 April the Tenth Army landed at Hagushi on the west coast, almost unopposed, and by 4 April had cut the island in two. On 6–7 April the Japanese struck the fleet with hundreds of kamikaze aircraft and sent the battleship Yamato on a sortie without air cover; carrier aircraft sank it on 7 April. The north of the island was cleared by 22 April. In the south the Americans met the fortified line through Naha, Shuri and Yonabaru, where the fighting was positional and savage: flame-throwing tanks led infantry against caves that had to be destroyed one by one, and the Japanese neither took prisoners nor generally surrendered. American troops entered Naha's suburbs on 12 May. Shuri fell at the turn of May and June, and the Naha airfield was taken in early June. Buckner was killed by artillery fire on 18 June while visiting a forward post, and major combat operations ended on 21 June. On 22 June Ushijima and his chief of staff killed themselves rather than surrender.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Ushijima's decision not to contest the beaches but to hold the fortified south, using caves and ridges, forced the Americans into costly frontal assaults: the Americans advanced only about 6 kilometres in the south between early April and late May. When Shuri could no longer be held, the army withdrew to the southern tip rather than fight a decisive battle there; the museum describes this as a choice to wage a bloody war of attrition, in the area where civilians had taken refuge. The Japanese command's reliance on mass suicide attacks at sea made the battle as costly for the navy as for the army. American commanders relied on the quantity and quality of their equipment, advancing in waves by day under heavy artillery support.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The battle for the Shuri line, from late April to the end of May, decided the campaign. Once Shuri fell, the defenders were exhausted and confined to the southern tip; Britannica notes that the Japanese lost Okinawa because they ran out of caves and boulders from which to fight and men to do the fighting.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The United States took Okinawa, at an enormous price on both sides. Both commanding generals died. Very few Japanese soldiers surrendered. The kamikaze attacks sank most of the American ships lost in the battle, and the navy suffered heavily.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The civilian population of Okinawa suffered catastrophically: Britannica writes that it was reduced by perhaps a quarter, with men, women and children killed in the fighting or ordered by the Japanese military to commit suicide, in some cases with a grenade given to a family to detonate when capture seemed near. The Peace Memorial Museum writes that civilian deaths far exceeded military ones: civilians were killed by shelling, starvation and malaria, by suicide, and by retreating Japanese troops, and in some caves Japanese soldiers killed civilians or forced them into mass suicide. The savagery of the battle shaped American expectations of an invasion of the home islands, which planners now expected to be terribly costly.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A defence in depth, from caves and ridges, can make every advance costly even against overwhelming firepower. Attrition at sea from suicide attacks can match the cost of the land battle. A battle fought among a civilian population makes civilians among its principal victims, and a military that orders civilians to die rather than surrender multiplies the catastrophe.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources give different figures for civilian deaths and military losses, and date the end of the battle to 21 or 22 June. Britannica records that American naval officers at first understated the effectiveness of the kamikaze attacks. The National WWII Museum and Britannica both link the battle's cost to American planning for the invasion of Japan, while the Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum presents the battle from the perspective of Okinawans, as a “Typhoon of Steel” in which the Japanese army's conduct was itself a cause of civilian deaths.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the planning, the commanders, the course of the battle, the kamikaze campaign, the civilian deaths and the battle's significance for the invasion of Japan. The National WWII Museum gives the purpose of the battle, the landing, the Shuri line, the kamikaze attacks, Buckner's death and the civilian toll. The Okinawa Prefectural Peace Memorial Museum's English guide and exhibit text give the Okinawan civilians' experience; its figures are not used.

Klaus Sommer: Erlebtes beim Endkampf um Berlin April/Mai 1945 (eyewitness account, in German)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In January 1945 the Red Army broke out of its bridgeheads on the Vistula, took Warsaw and advanced to the Oder, where by early February it stood about 65 kilometres from Berlin. German civilians fled west in their millions, joined by concentration camp prisoners forced on death marches, many of whom died. Stalin then halted the advance, and the Soviets cleared their flanks in Pomerania and Silesia.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Stalin mistrusted the Western Allies and wanted to take Berlin first; LeMO calls the capture of the German capital the declared aim of the Soviet leadership. When the Western Allies crossed the Rhine and approached the city in early April, he accelerated the attack. Hitler and committed Nazis had no option but to fight on, and many German soldiers fought in fear of what the Soviets would do in Germany after what German forces had done in the Soviet Union.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Soviet aim was to take Berlin and end the war. The main thrust was divided between Marshal Georgy Zhukov's 1st Belorussian Front and Marshal Ivan Konev's 1st Ukrainian Front, in what became a race for the city. The Germans aimed only to prolong the war.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Seelow Heights west of the Oder were the only place where the Germans had any hope of stopping the Soviets, and were fortified; beyond them there was little between the Soviets and Berlin. The city, repeatedly bombed, had few fixed defences, but its ruined streets favoured the defenders and made the final advance slow.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Soviets massed one of the largest concentrations of military power ever seen, with Zhukov's and Konev's fronts joined by Marshal Konstantin Rokossovsky's 2nd Belorussian Front in the north. The German defenders were shattered formations, stragglers and the Volkssturm militia of teenagers and old men, with Hitler Youth units, armed with the Panzerfaust; LeMO adds Waffen-SS units and improvised police formations, short of ammunition and fuel. A defender's account describes one sector held by a scratch force of interpreters, Volkssturm, alert units and police, short of automatic weapons.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: German intelligence had detected the Soviet build-up, but Hitler refused to believe the reports. The Germans withdrew their defenders from the first line of trenches at the Seelow Heights just before the Soviet barrage.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 16 April Zhukov's front attacked at the Seelow Heights. The barrage fell on empty trenches, and searchlights meant to blind the defenders silhouetted the attackers; Zhukov sent in his tanks before a breakthrough had been made, and they struggled on churned ground. Konev's attack further south succeeded, and on the fourth day the German line at Seelow broke. On 20 April Rokossovsky joined the attack and Soviet shells began to fall on the city. Hitler forbade retreat and ordered attacks by units that scarcely existed. By 25 April Berlin was encircled by Konev's and Zhukov's fronts. The Red Army fought through the city house by house, demolishing buildings that held defenders. Hitler killed himself on 30 April, after learning that the last relief attempt, by Wenck's Twelfth Army, had been broken off near Potsdam; that day a Soviet banner flew on the Reichstag, which French volunteers of the Waffen-SS had helped defend. On 2 May the garrison surrendered; Germany capitulated at Reims on 7 May and in Berlin-Karlshorst the next day.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Stalin's decision to split the attack between Zhukov and Konev manufactured a race for Berlin; he taunted Zhukov with giving the city to Konev, and later gave Zhukov the honour of taking the Reichstag. Britannica writes that both marshals were willing to accept enormous casualties and inflict colossal damage, and that Stalin's fixation on the symbolic Reichstag cost many Soviet lives. Zhukov's decision to send in his tanks before a breakthrough added to his losses. Hitler's refusal to allow retreat let the German Ninth Army be encircled.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The breaking of the Seelow Heights on the fourth day of the battle opened the road to Berlin, and the encirclement of the city on 25 April sealed its fate.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Berlin fell to the Red Army, and with it the Third Reich; the general surrender of German forces followed within a week. Losses on all sides were very heavy, and the city lay in ruins.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: German civilians and refugees trapped in the city suffered terribly: boys were sent to the front, civilians caught deserting were executed, and Soviet fire took no account of civilian lives. LeMO describes some two million inhabitants sheltering in cellars and bunkers, and SS squads shooting civilians and soldiers suspected of weakening resistance under a Führer order of 22 April. Soviet soldiers committed rape and sexual violence against German women on a vast scale; the IWM describes it as effectively state-sanctioned. The Soviet victory, the IWM notes, came from the greatest mass mobilisation in history and the immense sacrifice of the Soviet people.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Political goals, the race for Berlin and the symbolic Reichstag, can override military economy and multiply the cost of an operation. Urban assault against even scratch defenders is slow and destructive. A war waged as a war of annihilation ends in vengeance on the attacker's own civilians.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the battle from 16 April (the IWM and LeMO, counting the Seelow Heights) or from 20 April (Britannica, counting the fighting for the city). They give different figures for the forces and for military and civilian losses, which the IWM notes are almost impossible to calculate for civilians. The IWM discusses why German soldiers fought to the end; Klaus Sommer's account, set down after the war, shows defenders clinging to official promises of relief armies until the last day, and those who tried to avoid the fighting treated as traitors. Britannica stresses the cost of Stalin's fixation on the Reichstag. No Soviet-side source was read.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Robert Rumble's account for the Imperial War Museums gives the Vistula–Oder offensive, Stalin's decisions, the Seelow Heights, the encirclement, the street fighting, the violence against civilians and the end of the war. John Swift's Britannica article gives the forces, the race between Zhukov and Konev, the urban fighting, the suffering of civilians and the surrender. LeMO, the German Historical Museum's online history, gives the German side of the battle, and its eyewitness series the account of Klaus Sommer, born in 1927, who fought in the city as a young soldier in his father's sector; the opinions in it are his own. Their force figures are not used.
